subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as former U.S. President Franklin Delano Roosevelt once said in *Combats pour demain*, to govern means keeping the scales of justice the same for everyone. In fact, these words could very well have been part of the Budget Speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), because they reflect the underlying philosophy of this Budget.
During the past few days, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the comments of Hon. Members on the Budget brought down a week ago by the Minister of Finance. Mr. Speaker, I think it is appropriate to point out that this first Budget is a courageous, realistic and above all fair reflection of the broad economic proposals made by the Government last fall, with a view to stimulating the economic renewal asked for by the vast majority of Canadians.
The basic goal of the Budget proposals is to encourage the initiative of Canadian entrepreneurs, to improve Government effectiveness and to put our financial house in order. In making these proposals, the Government has also acknowledged its responsibility for social programs, and it has taken this rigorous approach in order to be in a position to discharge its responsibility to the less advantaged in our society.
Unlike previous governments, we decided last November and in the Budget before the House today, to take immediate steps to control a deficit that we felt had become a veritable threat to the Government's ability to play its true role and that was draining the energy of the private sector of our economy. We have always maintained, and we still do today, that not governments but private enterprise creates that wealth we need to provide for economic growth and create the jobs Canadians need.
A government cannot act effectively if it has to spend $20 billion or more annually to pay the interest on the national debt. More than 20 per cent of the Government's total expenditure will be used to service the national debt during this financial year. Canadian entrepreneurs cannot find the investment money they need if they must constantly compete with the Government on the capital markets.
We have decided to break this vicious circle. In fact, Canadians have congratulated this Government on the courage it has shown in this respect. The constant upward spiralling of the structural deficit could no longer be tolerated. As a percentage of the gross national product, the deficit rose from 16.6 per cent in 1974-75 to 45.2 per cent in 1984-85. The overall impact of our Budget proposals will be to reduce the deficit by $4.4, $8.3 and finally, $20.1 billion, respectively, over the next three financial years.
As a result of the steps taken by the Government last November, we have been able to cut $8.3 billion in Government spending over three financial years. The Budget brought
5218

May 30, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Masse
down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) will bring about an additional reduction of SI2.1 billion over the same period.
The Government has realized it could not ask Canadian taxpayers to take on the entire burden of reducing the deficit. It had to set an example by controlling its own spending and by making a systematic study of every one of its programs and activities. The expected levelling off of the deficit will be largely the result of the Budget cutbacks we have introduced. We are particularly concerned about the cumulative effect of Budget deficits. Less than 20 years ago, the cumulative deficit or national debt reached $18 billion. Today, it is nearly $200 billion, and this progression could not be allowed to continue.
It will become clear that the Government has not merely paid lip service to the need for reducing this crushing deficit, but has taken steps to deal with it.
We made this decision, Mr. Speaker, because we believe that the vast majority of Canadians wanted us to do so. When they entrusted the Progressive Conservative Party with a mandate for economic renewal, they did so in the knowledge that they were asking for a solution to a serious problem, a solution that could not longer be postponed indefinitely. Since last fall, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), the Minister of Finance, my colleagues and myself have been conducting consultations with all groups of our society. More than ever, we remain convinced that the vast majority of Canadians not only support our economic proposals but are indeed prepared to shoulder their part of the load in dealing with this country's finances.
Mr. Speaker, we are keenly aware of the fact that this Budget demands sacrifices by all members of our society, and we believe that all Canadians will acknowledge that this effort is necessary. We know that Budget cutbacks will have an impact on certain groups in our population, but our proposals have in no way tampered with the Government's social commitment which it sees as sacred. We have taken this approach precisely to make sure that in the coming years we will be in a position to protect the needy. In my judgment, we would not live up to that commitment if we were to let ever rising expenditures for certain programs grow unchecked. We would then be ignoring a basic fact-the Government's financial resources are not unlimited.
A few speakers in this debate seemed to imply that the Budget measures advocated by the Government would be unduly favourable to certain groups in society at the expense of others. I quite agree with all my colleagues that many of the provisions announced last week will have a very positive impact on entrepreneurs in the Canadian private sector, particularly with respect to small and medium-sized businesses. Far from feeling guilty about this favourable prejudice, Mr. Speaker, we are proud of it.
We believe that our Budget measures will prove to be a historic new trend in the Government's approach to economic
recovery and job creation. It reflects the change of attitude we promised Canadians last fall and stems from our vision of society.
The Government does not believe that the fairness of its Budget ought to be assessed only in terms of taxes imposed on a group of taxpayers or benefits given to another group. In our estimation, justice lies in the equitable sharing of responsibilities within the scope of a common objective.
The Budget incentives for Canadian businesses-the once-in-a-lifetime capital gains exemption, new pension plans provisions designed to spur investment in small and medium-sized businesses, and the small and medium-sized businesses exemption from the temporary corporate surtax, to name just a few-attest to the wide-ranging responsibilities given to the private sector. We are quite sure that the private sector will meet our expectations and that all Canadians will benefit from its contribution. In our opinion, Canadian entrepreneurs rather that Governments and public officials must channel most investments. We also believe that because they are prepared to take risks and work to achieve their goal, those entrepreneurs properly deserve to benefit from their own initiatives. It has been years and years since our business community got such a vote of confidence from Government.
In keeping with this vision of society whereby private sector interests have become partners of the State, the Government was prompted-in the Budget strategy under consideration today-to steer a new historic course in a sector which, I suggest, is just as vital to our collective existence as Canadians, namely arts and culture. This Budget marks the beginning of a new artistic and cultural era within Canadian society, not only because it offers lasting support, but rather as a result of its approach and its specific provisions. Mr. Speaker, I would be remiss if I failed to point out that, for the first time ever, a Government gives priority to this field of activity in an economic strategy document.
We formally acknowledge that arts and culture are not a negligible sector of our society and our economy, and it is that consideration which is the driving force behind all my endeavours as Minister responsible.
While it does not belittle their contribution to the quality of day-to-day life, the Budget and its provisions equate artistic and cultural activities with a genuine industrial sector. In 1980, the economic contribution of the artistic and cultural community amounted to between $14.7 and $16.8 billion and, in 1981, roughly 272,000 Canadians were gainfully employed in such activities. In terms of income, it ranked 11th among industrial sectors.
The formation of a Task Force on the Funding of the Arts is a Budget measure which faithfully reflects this new approach.
May 30, 1985

1 shall soon be able to disclose the names of the members and the terms of reference of this group. It is the first time the Minister of Finances and the Minister of Communications initiate such a joint action. The task force will submit to the Minister of Finance and to me a series of concrete recommendations on the various measures, including tax breaks, proposed to encourage the private sector to contribute more generously to artistic and cultural activities. True enough, we are looking for an increased participation by the corporations, but we must also find ways to convince ordinary Canadians to play a more active part too. Mr. Speaker, I should like to emphasize that this review and its orientation are in no way an indication of the government's intention to turn over to the private sector the main responsibility for supporting the arts, but rather a desire to increase the financial resources made available to participants within the Canadian artistic communities and cultural institutions.
As a matter of fact, the budget introduces several measures which are of immediate interest to Canadian artists. For instance, it proposes tax relief for visual artists through a change in the method of valuing their supplies, work-in progress and finished works of art. This means that when computing their income, they will no longer have to include the cost of such inventory. This change will simplify the tax affairs of individual artists and allow them to write off the costs involved in a work of art in the year they are incurred, rather than waiting until the work is sold.
We are currently considering other measures with the same outlook. Members of the artistic communities are more than creators, they are driving forces, a fact which our programs and policies should reflect. The Government wants to make sure that the financial resources whether they are provided by the public or by the private sector actually end up in the hands of Canadian men and women who can use them productively. This global approach to artistic and cultural financing is necessary in this period of budget restraint, for it will associate the public as a whole with the artistic community and extend the financial base of that industry. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, the multiplicity of funding sources is for the artistic community the best guarantee of its freedom.
In the area of radio broadcasting and telecommunications which also are part of my responsibility, the Government has put forward several major proposals. Having identified, as early as last November, the telecommunication industry as one of the main motors of economic growth, the Government has sought in its budget strategy to favour the tax environment within which corporations involved in this industry must operate. The research and development provisions especially will have a major impact on the telecommunication industry. An easing of the rules governing R and D will encourage the corporations involved in this industry to substantially increase their investments and help maintain our industry's reputation
The Budget-Mr. Masse
abroad as a source of quality programming. The budget also provides measures to help Canadian corporations involved in telecommunications and other high-tech industries become more competitive on international markets.
In the area of radio broadcasting, the budget proposes for instance to increase from 20 to 30 per cent the rate of capital cost allowance available to cable television systems for cable TV converters and descramblers. This new rate will apply to equipment purchased since last September, the start of the 1985 taxation year for most cable companies.
In this spirit of equitable sharing of responsibilities which I described a few minutes ago, the representatives of the radio broadcasting and telecommunication industries will have to co-operate with the Government in its efforts to put its financial house in order. Thus, the budget provides that my department will implement during the next financial year a series of measures aimed at recovering the costs of a number of services. Those measures should yield additional revenues of $ 15 million for the Treasury. The broadcasting and telecommunication industries will assume the operating costs of the CRTC and relevant regulating costs. The David Florida Laboratory of the Department which has been testing satellites and advanced technological products will also review its schedules of user fees to recover as soon as possible its entire costs.
Those are examples, Mr. Speaker, of the great equity of this budget. On one hand, the government has recognized that it was essential to encourage and promote the private sector in Canada, but it also makes sure that all Canadians will not have to assume the cost of services used essentially by specific concerns.
With respect to the basic principles which are part of our socio-political fabric as those dealing with social security, arts and culture, our government provides a continuity in the spirit of Canadian traditions. However, we have undertaken since September last to find new avenues and solutions. We have chosen to break free from a past the legacy of which is a financial disaster, adversarial relations in our society and intergovernmental relations lacking a minimum of respect. In this regard, this budget breaks off with the past. It rejects the notion of a society made up of diverging interest groups intent on destroying the system and grasping privileges and benefits. On the contrary, since last autumn we are trying to abolish that adversary system and to create at the social and political levels a new spirit of association and co-operation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Questions and comments. The Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to put a question to the Minister. Why has the Government tried to control the deficit rather than unemployment? Why the fight against the deficit rather than unemployment? I think that you are putting the cart before the horse! Why has the Government decided to reduce the deficit and not unemployment? In

May 30, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Masse
British Columbia where 1 live there is 15 per cent of unemployment and we are not trying to control the deficit-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in reply to the Hon. Member, 1 would say it is because we believe that the deficit in largely responsible for unemployment. As I told you, the public debt was $18 billion 20 years ago. The previous government, under the instigation of the NDP, decided to increase the deficit to reduce unemployment. As a result, our national debt has almost reached $200 billion. Today, almost 25 per cent of our revenues is used to pay interest. Such a policy has given us 1.5 million of unemployed in Canada. We believe that the other policy is sound, that is to reduce the deficit, to stimulate the economy while creating jobs through the private sector rather than public programs responsible for huge deficits.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as usual I listened very closely to the Minister's speech.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You were reading the paper!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Listen, you have to choose: either I will not listen to you or I will. I am listening carefully. I did not go to the trouble of coming here and listening to the Minister in order to shout at him. I was in my office when I saw that the Minister opposite whom I sit as a critic, was going to speak so as a courtesy I came in to listen to him and I intend to ask him questions.
I would like first to ask him about the rather troubling statement that was made by a very worthy lady, the Hon. Member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mrs. Bertrand). I do not believe that lady, a newly elected Member in this House, would indulge in pure demagogy. She made a statement 1 find quite troubling, and I am asking myself this question: Was she speaking on behalf of the Government when she stated it was not bound to all of its promises, that after all what importance does it have? Senior citizens will lose some $100 a year, which is not quite fair. And what does that amount to per day, 365 days, $100 a year? We know those are hundreds of dollars taken away from senior citizens, who are the most needy in our society, who have not enjoyed in the past all our social programs, who built this country.
Therefore, I would like to know first whether the Hon. Member for Brome-Missisquoi was speaking on behalf of the Government, since she is the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister in charge of all those programs, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, (Mr. Epp)? And if it is true that the Government does not feel bound by its commitments, how is it then that the former Minister of National Defence, whom I still call my hon. friend, who had promised during the election campaign that no later than July there would be new uniforms-certainly a futile, needless expense-nevertheless managed to keep his promise? And we know that as early as next summer, that promise will be fulfilled at an extra cost of
$35 million for this year, and over $20 million next year, in addition to causing complete havoc in the Armed Forces.
How is it that they could find $50 million of extra money this year, and $100 million in the following years, to increase by 1,150 our troops in Germany, as of this year, at a time when troop reduction is being negotiated in Geneva? We in Canada are increasing them, and we find the money for it, but we do not have the money needed to help our senior Canadian citizens who certainly are the most in need. They certainly will not be getting from this budget unbelievable capital gains.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to see my Hon. colleague in this House today, rushing to his seat because the Minister of Communications is going to speak. But 1 had hoped his questions would have dealt with cultural affairs, broadcasting or communications in Canada.
But he is asking two questions. First, about election promises. The Hon. Member knows perfectly well, and his wide parliamentary experience should inspire him in that respect, that election promises made by political parties are government commitments, mandate commitments, and that it is over the whole of their mandate, when the parties go back before the electors, that the latter will pass judgment on the carrying out of their election platform. So we will see at the end of our mandate, and I can assure the Hon. Member that the commitments made by the Progressive Conservative Party before the Canadian people will have been fulfilled when we go back before them.
Second, the Hon. Member has mentioned uniforms. It is not my responsibility on behalf of the Government to engage in debate on national defence. But I would like to point out, after certain comments made by Members of his party a few minutes ago for instance concerning Government or programs in the economy, that on the one hand, members of our armed forces are entitled to programs that meet their needs, their wishes, their abilities, their pride. And second, that the implementation of that program will widely benefit the Quebec economy, because if I remember correctly, more than or close to 50 per cent of those uniforms will be manufactured by small and medium-sized businesses in Quebec. And to that extent, I do not understand why the Liberal Member indulges in demagogy when there is a real need in the textile industry in Quebec.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a question of the Minister based on his thorough and extensive knowledge of agriculture. The Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) said the Minister in his speech had the horse before the cart. I would like to ask the Minister if that is not the right place to put the horse?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I said the cart before the horse.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And is it not the case that the Liberals and the New Democratic Party have had the cart before the horse for
May 30, 1985

all these years, and it is those Hon. Members who have an economic mix-up because they believe Governments can create jobs and not the private sector? Would the Minister, out of his knowledge of agriculture, tell the Hon. Member of the New Democratic Party that the horse is supposed to be in front of the cart?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Perhaps there is something lost in the translation or perhaps it is my French, but I thought I said, "le chariot avant le bceuF'. That means, as far as I understand, the cart is before the horse not the horse before the cart.
[ Translation]

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not want to open a debate on the realities of agriculture in Canada, but 1 know for a fact that in a public budget, revenues must come before deficits if jobs are to be created.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I must advise Hon. Members that the ten-minute period for questions or comments has expired unless the House, by unanimous consent, wishes to continue. We shall resume debate.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have heard the Budget which was delivered here last week described as "sneaky, cruel, harsh" and "Draconian". 1 think there is another word I would use to describe this budget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Careful, John.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I would think this Budget is "crafty", Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Crass, too.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Crass and crafty. It was very craftily drawn, Mr. Speaker. I am not surprised that the Conservatives would bring in this kind of Budget. Every time the Conservatives govern in this country, we hear the old saying, "Tory times are tough times". As I watched last night the trek on to Ottawa from Vancouver back to the 1930s 1 could not only see the R. B. Bennett days formulating over on the other side of the House, but I could see something much more insidious and vicious. What I see in this Budget is a reinforcing and restructuring of the class system in this country. In fact, we are going back to a very class conscious society between the wealthy and the poor.
I would tend to call this budget "the Robin Hood Budget" with a twist. Where Robin Hood used to take from the rich to distribute to the poor, this Budget, this Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and this Government, takes from the poor to give to the wealthy of this country. When one looks closely at the measures in this Budget, the pension provisions, the federal sales tax provisions, the RRSP giveaways and the capital gains giveaways, the message is very clear. The Government is taking from those who have the least and giving to those who have the most. It is all based on the fallacy that when those
The Budget-Mr. Rodriguez
who have gorged themselves on the labour and fruits of those who are at the bottom end of the economic scale, somehow or other some of it will trickle down to the people at the bottom and jobs will be created.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The trickle-down theory.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Trickle-down theory, and it is liquid and amber coloured and I am running for cover, brother; I am not sticking around. People had better get out their umbrellas.
Let us look at the whole question of pensions, Mr. Speaker. One of the things this Budget does is reinforce the cynicism among people about politicians; when politicians are trying to get into office they make all sorts of promises. But lo and behold, once they have achieved office, they turn around and go against the very things they promised. We have many examples of that kind of cynicism building again in this Budget. We have examples of taking from the poor and giving to the wealthy. Look at deindexing. In 1980 the Conservative Party placed ads in newspapers across the country criticizing the Liberal Government. They said:
You've heard a lot about the Constitution lately, but how much have you heard about deindexing?
Deindexing is a system to guarantee that you'll pay higher federal income taxes year after year.
Deindexing would mean a massive tax increase for all Canadians.
Deindexing would raise a lot of money. Fast, $1.6 billion in the First year alone.
Deindexing would hit people living on low incomes the hardest.
The Progressive Conservative Party of Canada is providing the opposition.
Indexing was our idea in the first place.
And we are determined that you should continue to receive this fundamental protection against inflation.
But we need your help. It's time for all Canadians to speak up.
An important message from the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada.
The Tories placed those ads pointing out the dangers of deindexing. Now that they are in Government, what have they done? They have deindexed old age pensions, and old age pensioners are being asked to take up the first 3 per cent of inflation. This contradicts what they said in their public advertising campaign. This is in complete contradiction of what the Prime Minister said when he promised "complete indexing of old age pensions to the actual cost of living". What we see here is a direct attack on the principle of universality. Because of deindexation, the old age pensioners will receive $100 less next year and that will put them even further below the poverty line. The cumulative effect will be $203 the following year, and by 1990 seniors will be $512 further below the poverty line.
As well, Mr. Speaker, de-indexation contradicts the Tory promise that as soon as the Government's financial position allows, it will provide increased financial assistance to single senior citizens whose incomes are below the poverty line. So the Government puts these people below the poverty line, takes money away from middle and low income Canadians,

May 30, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Rodriguez
increases the federal sales tax and allows the poorest of the poor to fall even further below the poverty line.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Do you know what the word "honest" means?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But how does the Government treat high income earners? The Hon. Member across the floor says "be honest".

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Tell the truth.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He says they have kept the index on the GIS. I said that full indexing remains on the supplement. How do they treat the wealthy?

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order, please. Will the Hon. Member be polite enough to listen to the comments of the Hon. Member?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Thank you, Mr. Speaker. How does this Government treat the wealthy? Looking at RRSPs, those who earn $86,000 a year or more will now be allowed to increase their tax deductible RRSP contributions from $5,500 to $15,500. Where is the principle of deindexation there? The $15,500 will be fully indexed. There is no discounting of the first 3 per cent of inflation. It is fully indexed. These people can sock away the $15,000 each year plus the fully indexed cost of living. Do you know what that means? It means people in the 50 per cent a year bracket can pocket $5,000 more of what they earn. That is as much as some people in my riding live on. That is the Government's view of fairness!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Louder, I cannot hear you.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What will that cost the Government? Its own figures indicate that giveaway will cost $235 million. The Tories are taking that $235 million from the poor and middle income Canadians and transferring it directly to the wealthy.
You might ask how do they treat the person earning $30,000 with respect to RRSPs? Instead of allowing them to deduct up to 20 per cent of their income, they are cutting back so that they will only be allowed to deduct up to 18 per cent. On the one hand, we give upper income Canadians a bonanza, and on the other hand the people at the middle and lower income level get cut. Is that the Conservative sense of fairness?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, it is.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I suspect it is much more machiavellian. Right through this Budget we see a constant shifting of income from low and middle income Canadians to upper income Canadians. If there is an honest Conservative in the House, they will admit that.
From the Government's own figures, Mr. Speaker, by March 31, 1991, the children's benefit will be $635 million less than under the present program. This has to be a Titanic Budget: it is children and senior citizens first. They are taking $635 million out of the child benefit program of this country, as well as a massive $1.6 billion less for old age pension benefits, and what are they doing with it? What are they doing
with this theft from Canada's social programs? Are they doing something creative?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Giving it to the oil companies.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They say they are going to reduce the deficit. I know this Government has a fixation about reducing the deficit, just as Margaret Thatcher has a fixation about reducing the deficit, yet unemployment problems remain in Great Britain. We know that the Premier of British Columbia has a fixation with reducing deficits.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And they are getting bigger.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Deficits are getting bigger and unemployment is getting higher. There are no jobs for anyone in British Columbia. But when I hear about this fixation with deficits I am reminded of a quote by Kevin Doyle, the editor of Maclean's magazine. I would like to read that quote from the February 4, 1985 issue of Maclean's. It reads:
The preoccupation with the deficit has become a menace. The word has become a little-understood part of the jargon that men without imagination and governments without direction use to disguise their poverty of purpose. It is a blind to be drawn over any discussion of the real economic challenges that face us, as well as over any argument that threatens to disturb the comfortable, conventional maunderings of the uncaring.
I think that is a very appropriate way of describing the obsession of this Government and governments like it with the deficit. Is the most creative use that we can make of the money removed from the economy through the Budget to put it toward reducing the deficit, in spite of the fact that that completely contravenes and contradicts what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said on November 17? He said that money saved by retargeting social programs would not be used to reduce the deficit but redistributed to the neediest. Well, it is not being redistributed to the neediest, it is being given to the greediest in society.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Another area in which they have socked it to ordinary Canadians is in the deindexation of personal income tax. By 1990, as indicated in its own figures, the federal Government will collect $4.4 billion more in income tax revenue. On the other hand, corporations will receive $540 million next year and $2.2 billion by 1990 as a direct transfer. It is taken from those who have the least and given to those who are already enjoying a very low tax rate in the economy.
When I returned to the House in September of 1984, I was struck by the proliferation of powerful lobbies on the Hill. The oil companies have one of the most powerful lobbies. They pay very little tax, only 7 per cent in 1979. The Bankers' Association has a very powerful lobby. They float around in their pin-striped suits. The drug lobbies are getting what they want now, which will sock it to individuals who have the misfortune of being sick. The Manufacturers' Association has another very powerful lobby. It is time that we considered registering the lobbies on the Hill. This might be the appropriate time.
May 30, 1985

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There is no more regressive tax in any land than a sales tax because it does not take account of the ability of an individual to pay. It is a regressive tax which goes with a regressive Conservative Government. By 1990 the Government will collect $2.6 billion more in federal sales tax. Sales tax is being slapped on candy, confections, pet food, soft drinks, health goods, surgical and dental instruments, X-ray apparatus and films, wood-burning stoves, wind deflectors, heat pumps, solar heating panels, furnaces, insulating materials, wind generators, windmills, and other such goods. Having socked it to people who were trying to save on energy through the elimination of COSP, the Government has now socked it to them through federal sales tax.
The sneaky thing about this is that the federal sales tax is rolled into the price. Therefore, the provincial sales tax is applied on the total price, including the federal sales tax. We therefore have a tax on a tax. Ten per cent will be applied on those items. In fact, it increased by 1 per cent in November and will increase by 1 per cent in January. That is a 2 per cent increase in federal sales tax in the space of one year.
This Budget emphasizes and reinforces the class structure in the country. There is no minimum tax on the rich and the wealthy escape the puff-ball attempt to implement a surtax because, if they do not pay tax, they do not pay the surtax. According to the Budget, the surtax is to take in $550 million next year. However, on the other hand, through capital gains tax exemptions and RRSPs, it gives the wealthy $640 million in the same year.
A report prepared by the Department of Finance indicates that the removal of the capital gains tax means that Canada will be taxing its rich much more lightly than any other industrialized country in the world. The Government is determined to redistribute the wealth in the country from the poor to the wealthy. This Budget does not deal with the most important problem facing Canada, unemployment. In our paper Canada Unlimited, we have targeted unemployment. The Government has failed to deal with that most pressing problem. This Budget could very well add to the deficit as well as exacerbating unemployment.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to comment on the Hon. Member's speech. He refers to a Robin Hood Budget. That is the quaint phraseology which the business sector used to refer to the Budget of November, 1981. As the Hon. Member says, this is different because it is taking from the poor and giving to the rich. Would the Hon. Member accept the terminology "a sheriff of Nottingham Budget"?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would certainly accept that, Mr. Speaker. I recall that the MacEachen Budget was a serious attempt to redistribute wealth from the wealthy to those who needed it. We have never heard such a howling as went up across the country. The lobbies were in full bay. The Conservatives were part of that lobby group. The MacEachen Budget was forcibly put aside. This is a Robin Hood Budget with the Prime
The Budget-Mr. Rodriguez
Minister as Friar Tuck and the merry men of Nottingham. When the Budget was to be brought down, they were all in Europe. Phone calls were made to bring them back so that they could surround Robin Hood, Friar Tuck, and the merry men of Nottingham Forest. It was necessary to use the wide angle so that the folks across the country could see that they were indeed merry. Their merriment reached a peack when the Minister of Finance said that capital gains tax was being removed to a limit of $500,000. They stood to a person and applauded loudly. I think that is a fair indication of the kind of Budget this is. I think they ought to be very ashamed of this Budget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I grew up on a farm. We used to put blinders on horses so that the horses would not be able to see people on either side of them. It seems to me that the Member is taking that kind of approach to the Budget. You are not prepared to look at what is happening around Canada and what must happen on a broad base. Of course, if we use tunnel vision, we can pick out any particular item in the Budget and say that it has some serious negative impact. However, if you look at the over-all broad issues, it seems to me that with thousands of small business people in the country who employ one or two other people and others who would like to quit jobs now to enter into small business, there is a possibility and the opportunity for those people to run their own small business and take some initiative.
It seems to me that the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) is putting on blinders. He is not prepared to look at the impact of this Budget on the very small businessmen in his constituency. I have visited his constituency, and I know what kind of people live there. I ask the Hon. Member, who certainly spoke a lot about small business during the election, how he would approach the problem of trying to turn the economy around by including small business initiatives in his constituency and across the country?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member represents Saskatoon East. As a matter of fact, I have a letter from one of his constituents. She is a 48-year old single grandmother of seven with a small business. She wrote a letter dated May 24, 1985, to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). Let me read this letter in order to answer his impassioned plea about how the Budget helps small business:
Dear Mr. Wilson:
This is a letter about betrayal-the complete betrayal of the Canadian people by you and by your Party. Your actions since the September, 1984, election and the federal budget, have put the lie to everything you campaigned on during last summer's election campaign, while using the word "sincerity" dripping through every advertisement and speech. I knew then, and you have proven since, that this was honeyed venom.
This woman operates a small business. The letter goes on to point out how the Budget very seriously affects her business:
Until you are willing to listen to logic and reason from ordinary citizens in this country, and to make radical changes in this budget, as well as many of your other policies (not just bandaid measures), I am withdrawing completely from the payment of income tax, beginning immediately. Until you assign a decent

May 30, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Rodriguez
amount of the revenue earned by your government to the wellbeing of Canadian citizens who are now suffering with unemployment, and on fixed incomes, I am conscientiously objecting and will not be able to live with myself by contributing to your cavalier attitude and actions toward those who are suffering around me.
When listened to the Budget, I hoped that it would effectively deal with creating employment in areas like mine, which is suffering from 16 per cent unemployment. We do not have a private sector base.
I questioned how the Budget would provide an incentive for Falconbridge and Inco to hire more people. It does not provide that incentive. The Budget will not motivate those who deal in RRSPs to invest in my riding, because they are highly speculative. How will the capital gains tax exemption stimulate employment in my area? Those Canadians will simply sell what they have and buy a condominium in Florida. It will not help create employment and, therefore, I honestly say that while my hopes were high, they were dashed.
[ Translation]

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, our country has a wealth of natural resources and an extraordinary human potential. The major problem in the past was that the Government stifled personal initiative and killed all hopes of succeeding. That is the cause of our main problem and disastrous situation in this country. It is absolutely essential to restore confidence to the people in research and development, and I wonder what the Hon. Member is trying to sell us today. He has absolutely nothing to sell since he said that we must help the poor and the needy. We have nothing against this, but if you get to the point where your only throught is of helping the poor and the needy, you disrupt the system by preventing those who are able to succeed from doing so. Then, your businesses close down, there is no more money for the Government and people stop working. When people no longer work, they cannot pay taxes to the Government. I would like the Hon. Member to tell me where we shall find all this money if businesses close down and if the people stop working. That is my question. I do not know where that reasoning can lead you.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps the Hon. Member did not hear me. When the Government imposes a tax on pet food, soap and shampoo, regardless of the fact that people may not be able to afford it now, it is essentially punishing poor people. A sales tax is not progressive and simply dampens demand. It does not stimulate the economy at the consumer level.
The Budget seeks to inspire confidence in the rich. It does not matter if the poor have confidence and I suspect that if the Hon. Member is really interested in stimulating the economy, he would consider that.
I also pointed out that there is a disparity with respect to old age pensions. This year, the Government is taking $100 from old age pensioners. In my riding that is the only income for many old age pensioners because they worked for companies that never had a pension plan. They depend on that old age
pension, and when the Government removes $100 this year, the cumulative effect on them becomes $512.
[ Translation]

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very proud to have this opportunity, First of all, to offer my sincere congratulations to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) on bringing down a Budget on May 23 of this year that is realistic, effective and fair. I may add that I find it very exciting to be taking part in the Budget debate, considering its tremendous impact on job creation.
The Budget was so well received by tax experts and economists that it was even referred to by some as conservative, literally. A great deal of preparation went into this Budget, but I think that the Budget papers especially reflect some very positive aspects for small- and medium-sized businesses. This Budget has a direct impact on business people. On May 23, the Progressive Conservative Government brought new hope to small- and medium-sized businesses, and the time has come for the private sector to regain confidence in its potential. It is time for businessmen and women to show what they can do. Our party was put in power to bring about a change for the better, and that is what it is doing. As far as policy is concerned, this change represents a sizeable break with the past, and that is reflected in the Budget.
This Budget has benefitted from the most extensive round of pre-budget consultations ever held in Canadian history. Whereas before, the independence of private entrepreneurs was questionable, to say the least, they are now being encouraged to become more actively involved than ever before in increasing awareness of their strength and potential at the local, national and regional level. It is this involvement that will give our economy the clout it needs at the international level.
It would be too easy to say that the Budget is giving the private sector a chance to change the present state of affairs. However, it is challenging entrepreneurs to take the iniative. There is no longer any reason for the lack of initiative shown by business people so far in this country. Various business-oriented incentives have removed the taint from the word "profit". Creativity and innovation are high on the priority list, and productivity will at last be rewarded.
Yes, this Budget favours private enterprise. Yes, it is giving the private sector the tools it needs to overcome its economic stagnation. Yes, the entrepreneur must get involved. It is a must. It is a real must. Otherwise, the Budget will be useless.
Good intentions are not enough to bring about change. We need action! We need immediate, intelligent and genuine action. How are the measures this Budget contains going to help private enterprise prosper? Very simple: it will have to
May 30, 1985

adopt as its motto the slogan of every good manager: product, quality and price.
We must make our products competitive. Well before they become obsolete, we must already be developing new ones. The Budget has introduced changes to the definition of research and development so that more enterprises will be able to benefit. Our small- and medium-sized businesses have not lost their sense of creativity, but it must be revitalized.
If we are not active in certain areas, perhaps we should ask ourselves why. Hi-tech companies are scarce in Quebec, that is a fact. But where are the incentives for such firms? Language and fiscal barriers, for instance, have tended to discourage companies and investment in this area. Although we may not get those hi-tech companies overnight, we can at least start by creating a climate that is favourable to their growth and development.
Our firms are just as competent as others in foreign countries. We have here in Canada everything we need to compete on international markets. Our efforts must be directed towards export products, but beware, they must bear the seal of quality. We do not stand to gain much encouragement by comparing the number of American-Canadian car recalls to that of imported cars. We do know that the standards are identical in both cases.
Canadian companies have to set their own production targets and, as required, replace obsolete equipment, expand or bring in new blood. I am proud to remind the House that small- and medium-sized businesses need look no further than the Budget to find provisions under which they can obtain the funds needed for such investments.
Businessmen now see a way out of their stagnant situation. Conditions will improve, businesses will gain strength, and at last they can see the light at the end of the tunnel.
Small and medium-sized company management fully appreciate that the incentive measures announced on May 23 will improve the economic and financial outlook. Success rather than effort will be rewarded. Every businessman will be goaded into action by the new Government tax measures.
And we know what those measures are.
One. The lifetime $500,000 capital gains exemption. This additional financial input will unable management to direct those funds towards better planning of future business. Close to one million Canadians will benefit from this measure, an open invitation to invest in small and medium-sized businesses.
Two. Budget measures make it easy for pension funds to invest in small and medium-sized company capital stock. RRSPs and registered retirement income funds can also be channelled into private Canadian companies. Even the labour movement is urged to invest in businesses. This can be a reliable pool of capital for small and medium-sized businesses, a new source a capital funding.
The Budget-Mr. M.R. Tremblay
Third. The fully refundable tax credit on the first $2 million in eligible expenditures on research and development each year. As you know, Mr. Speaker, small and medium-sized companies were so far limited to 40 per cent of the tax credit and most of them could not really afford to go into research and development. The funds required to maintain day-to-day operations did not leave enough leeway to consider investment in research.
Four. The extension of the small business bond program, a readily available source of funds for companies temporarily strapped for cash.
Five. Unemployment insurance premiums will be frozen in 1986, leaving more money in the hands of companies. A thorough review of the UI program will be undertaken later.
Six. Small and medium-sized companies will be exempt from the 5 per cent corporate surtax.
Seven. Business fluctuations often made it difficult for small business owners to make regular contributions to an RRSP for their retirement years. Henceforth they will be able to carry forward unused contribution room for seven years.
Eight. A new tax credit to individuals investing in the Quebec Solidarity Fund.
Nine. The documents tabled with the Budget contain a proposition aimed at significantly reducing the basic federal tax of small companies-from 15 to 11 per cent.
The total amount of money that these measures will make available for the SMB's may help investment within the individual business in improving manufacturing processes, updating equipment, increasing production, paying interests on loans, and so on. The previous Government was unable to motivate the business community and neglected private enterprise. But this Government has brought down a political budget which by itself scorns the complexities of a strictly accounting budget.
The end result of all those measures will be a decrease in the burden of the SMB's. In turn, their financial resources will increase. New firms which to this day had difficulty attracting investment will from now on have all the support they need. The new budget will have reached its goal, which is to be a catalyst for the Canadian economy.
I for one am committed to using in my beautiful constituency of Quebec East all the energy needed to get business people involved, and I urge my colleagues to do the same, and make entrepreneurs aware that their daily involvement is vital to the success of this budget. I would even offer my support to other Hon. Members who defend that view.
Crippled businesses must be revived at all costs, business leaders must concentrate on creating jobs and carrying out the research work needed in order that the economy may go forward, for humanitarian if not philantropic reasons. Humanitarian, because even with the profit motive, a business can

May 30, 1985
The Budget-Mr. M.R. Tremblay improve working conditions and help the cause of the unemployed. Profit is defined in the dictionary as: "An increase in the goods one owns, or the improvement in status resulting from some activity". I would even suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the concept of labour should be added to that definition.
We can say that the Government has honoured its commitment to ensure economic revival and job creation. What better way of helping the SMB's generate jobs and new R&D activities than our Progressive Conservative budget? The Government has realized that the only way to give the economy a forward push was to strenghten the SMB's and avoid hindering their development. As many of us have already said in this House, I will repeat, Mr. Speaker, that the Budget brought down by the Minister of Finance is realistic, efficient and fair. The Budget does recognize that Canadians individually and collectively will be able to achieve the desired economic progress. At the same time, it does recognize that there is no wonder solution, but that a balanced program involving growth, better management, decreased expenditures, and tax increases, is a starting point for the reorganization of our finances and the nationalization of overall Government management.
The Government has put the emphasis on the private sector because it strongly believes that stable and meaningful jobs are better provided by business people. This Budget is clearly a step in the right direction towards an economic renewal.
You will note, Mr. Speaker, that in my remarks up to this point, I have dealt mainly with that aspect of the Budget that promotes private initiative. This was the first of the three areas in which the Budget proposed measures for economic renewal. The two other areas are improving Government effectiveness and controlling the national debt. The Budget will enable the Government to better manage the affairs of the state. We have dealt with a few simplifications of Government programs, and finally the Government's financial responsibility takes precedence together with its will to cut down on the huge size of Government. The Government, in its capacity as a trustee, will reduce the funding of many Departments and review several programs, in order to better allocate whatever funds are available.
Mr. Speaker, the Government also is exercizing restraint at the financial responsibility level, by proceeding to reduce subsidies, to rationalize the public service, even eliminating 30,000 jobs, to improve cash management, to dispose of surplus buildings-to close down plants manufacturing products for which there is no demand-to increase cost recovery, to move towards on improved and renewed budget process.
The reduction in the huge size of government will be achieved not only by rationalizing the public service and various Government programs, but also by privatizing Crown corporations. Thirteen of them will no longer compete against small businesses. After they are sold, disbanded or integrated into existing departments, small businesses will be better able
to develop in those specific areas. This will help restore their faith in the Government.
As much as small businessmen used to be suspicious of the Government, they will now be motivated to succeed. Their competition will no longer be subsidized by the Government. We are opening up avenues for conscientious and hard-working businessmen.
The last point I wish to raise is the matter of getting our national debt under control as soon as possible. This Budget counters the effects of the heavy legacy left by the previous Government. All those who have positive or negative reactionary tendencies should keep in mind that this Budget is only a partial aspect of the general policies of our Federal Government. However, the Budget projects our image to foreign countries. For instance, the Western Energy Accord will restore confidence in Canada at the international level. It will stimulate the flow of foreign currency into Canada. Believe me, Mr. Speaker, as far as investments are concerned, whether the bills are blue, red or green and measure 3 by 5 inches or 7 by 8 inches, we shall accept all of them equally for the simple reason that this is what we want from other countries. We do not want foreign workers who are supposedly better qualified to manage our businesses because many of our business people are said to lack intellectual vigour. We have the human resources we need. We only have to identify them, to go and get them and urge them to do their share in improving the economy.
Our Budget represents a major break with the past and gives us some hope of stabilizing our deficit. A reduction of the deficit means a decrease in interest rates for borrowers, which is economically beneficial for the Government, for businesses, and also for individuals. A reduction of the deficit also brings down inflation, which decreases the need for indexation, but let us leave this matter aside for the moment. Let us simply say that the approach chosen by the Government is a gradual one and that the Budget is the first step. However, the Nielsen Task Force is still considering ways to reduce spending.
In conclusion, I wish to emphasize that our Government is taking seriously the mandate for change it has received last September 4. Emphasis is on job creation, growth and Government responsibility. We are fighting three things: unemployment, unemployment, unemployment. Unemployment among young people, unemployment among the middle-aged and unemployment among people on the eve of retirement.
Mr. Speaker, I repeat that this Budget will prove effective by creating new jobs for Canadians. It will no longer be politicians and bureaucrats who decide for Canadians where to invest and how to create jobs. The initiative will now be taken by the people, not by the Government.
Mr. Speaker, I have the great pleasure to confirm that our Government has taken the measures required to create a

May 30, 1985
climate which will result in increased investments and more jobs. Our Budget asks Canadians to translate their ideas and energies into action in order to make of this country what we want for ourselves and our children.
Our job as Members of Parliament is clear. We, in the Government, must send to the business sector this message, on which I shall conclude my remarks: Take advantage of this opportunity! The Government has placed you in the forefront. It is up to you to put Canada back on its feet and make it competitive. You are competent, dynamic, creative, knowledgeable, proud, responsible, conservative and progressive! Finally, Mr. Speaker, I realize that they are all that as much as myself.

subsubtopic: SOCCER RIOT FATALITIES-CONDEMNATION OF FANS' VIOLENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday's violent attack which led to the deaths of 41 individuals at the European Cup finals soccer game between Liverpool of England and Juventus of Italy was a brutal, savage, and barbaric act. It is an act which has, unfortunately, begun to appear on the international sports stage, particularly in soccer, with all too much frequency. This is a cause for great concern.

May 30, 1985
This violence needs to be condemned in the strongest possible terms. However, most important, such senseless and immoral events need to be brought to an immediate end. Strict and swift reprisals must be taken against any culprit wishing to engage in such perverse displays. Responsibilities on the part of sports organizations and Governments must be clearly defined and carried out.
There are those who suggest that harsh penalties might hurt the game of soccer. As a progressive society we cannot stand idly by and risk the lives of innocent individuals for the protection and sake of a soccer game on the field. Our priorities need to be clear, and vigorously pursued. Violence in the stands must be fully cleaned up before the whistle starting a game can be blown.
Canada has a unique opportunity to play a vital role in ensuring that respectability and civility are returned to sports competitions. Our record for sports-related incidents is highly envied throughout the world. Thus we can and should be sports ambassadors of goodwill.

subsubtopic: EMBARGO ON HOG SHIPMENTS TO UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the States of North Dakota, South Dakota, Nebraska, Iowa, and Wisconsin recently placed an embargo on Canadian hogs saying that Canadian hogs contain traces of chloramphenicol, an antibiotic which has been recently banned from use in the U.S. Despite increased monitoring, not a single positive indication of the drug has been found in Canadian meat. Canada performs monitoring interprovincially, as well, and no traces have been found, even though the drug is used on occasion under veterinary order.
This embargo, coupled with the recent tariff increase which the U.S. has unilaterally placed on Canadian hogs going to the U.S., will have disastrous effects on our pork industry. Last year 96,000 hogs were shipped to South Dakota alone.
Chloramphenicol can cause aplastic anemia. Some researchers in the U.S. estimate one in 50,000 people may be genetically susceptible to the disease if chloramphenicol is used. The incidence of anemia, however, is no higher in Canada than in the U.S.A. where the drug has been banned, so the reason for causing pork to be stopped at the border is economic rather than medical or scientific. I call into question the whole affair.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF LAYOFFS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to call the attention of the House to the layoffs announced yesterday by Canadian National Railways, where 4,100 employees out of the main shop's workforce of 5,500 will be laid off for an extra four weeks this summer over and above the usual summer shutdown.
Apart from my customary objection to this practice of the CNR, whereby it seeks to balance out its books on the backs of young workers and their families, it is interesting to note that the reason given for this layoff was flat traffic forecasts. I find it ironic, indeed, that within a week of the Budget, and some six months after the November 8 statement which was supposed to create all kinds of confidence in the economy and set the country rolling again, we have the major railway in the country laying off people because it does not expect the economy to be moving at all. It does not have enough confidence in the Government's own Budget to be putting people to work for the full year to prepare the rolling stock for the goods that will have to be moved. If the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has as much confidence in his Budget as he really says he does, then I suggest he get on the phone to the president of the CNR, Mr. LeClair, and tell him to cancel the shutdown and keep people working.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had the opportunity this morning of listening to the interventions of a number of government Members who were prepared to stand in their places and tell the people of Canada that they were elected to fight a deficit on the backs of senior citizens from coast to coast. 1 want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that this Government has clearly shown through this Budget for the first time a kind of cold blooded, blue blooded attack, not only on the middle class but also on those in our society who can least afford to a pay.
This Government is so arrogant that when it tabled the budget documents it even thought it could turn maple leafs into blue maple leafs.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As far as I know, the Canadian flag is a red maple leaf representing Canada from coast to coast. The Government has even gone to the extent, in its hungry search for publicity, of turning the Canadian flag into a blue flag indicative of the blue blooded, cold hearted, iceberg approach which the Tories have taken to deficit reduction.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are setting women's rights back one hundred years.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Member has said I have set women's rights back one hundred years. 1 want to tell the Member that this Budget has set the rights of senior citizens back one hundred years because the Government has a Finance Minister who has the gall to stand here in the House and tell senior citizens that their purchasing power will be reduced by $500 a year as a result of this Government's budget cut-backs. Those are the very senior citizens currently living below the poverty line who are being expected to bear the brunt of an economy which offers tax write-offs to the very, very rich.
Congratulations. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has now said that anybody who leaves the country at any time can now write off $100 in tax free goods. Do you think the senior citizens who are scraping the bottom of the economic barrel can afford to travel on a regular basis, Mr. Speaker? No, they cannot. The beneficiaries of that particular tax write-off will be the business people who already have enough write-offs.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) has quite clearly shown us how the half a million dollar capital gains tax write-off will put $125,000 into the pockets of the very rich. At the same time, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) have the nerve to stand here in the House and say that senior citizens should bear the burden of that measure.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That hollow argument is somehow saying that this particular initiative will result in job creation. We know the direct impact of this Budget-we have seen some of the results in the announcement today on Canadian National-, will be to cut 125,000 to 150,000 Canadian jobs. I plead with government Members, if there is to be job creation as a direct result of this Budget, to table the documents in the House, to table the projections in the House and to table the assessments in the House. It is quite clear that the Minister of Finance has taken a Pontius Pilate approach to job creation by saying to young people, "I wash my hands of this". There are 1.4 million people who are not working, yet the Minister of Finance has the nerve to cut back on job creation protection and projections through the federal Government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He is helping young people.

May 30, 1985

[ Translation]

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member says that he is helping young people. I am young myself, much younger than the Hon. Member who has just spoken, and I should like to ask him directly how this Budget will help in view of the 125,000 or so jobs that will disappear as a direct result of the Budget measures.
Mr. Speaker, it is clear that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and his "true blue" colleagues of this Conservative Government-"true blue" because of their blood and because of the "Blues" they are inflicting-do not care whether our senior citizens freeze next winter, because they are more eager to fight against the deficit "on the backs" of our senior citizens than to create jobs for our young people.
On the Liberal side, Mr. Speaker, we had hoped for a Budget which would have directly resulted in job creating schemes. Alas, it was in vain. What we see here is a Government which is prepared to give a $125,000 cash bonanza to every Canadian earning over $100,000.
Mr. Speaker, it is a fact that only 4 per cent of Canadians can benefit from the Government's initiative to exempt from tax the first $500,000 in capital gains. I repeat, only 4 per cent of Canadians is able to benefit from this initiative, and it is our senior citizens, our underprivileged and middle income people who will foot the bill.
During the campaign, many Canadians believed the promises of the Government. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said that universality was a sacred trust, when the Prime Minister stood in the House of Commons and said that indexation would not be touched, people believed him. They thought him to be a man of his word, but the record and this Budget clearly show otherwise. They show that the Government is prepared in the most insidious way to reach out into the pockets of not only senior citizens, but of our children.
1 received a telephone call this morning from a gentleman in my riding who is very involved in a local candy factory, Allan Dancy. Most of the Members on the government side may not know that 8,000 people are employed coast to coast in the confectionary industry. Those people are facing massive layoffs as a direct result of the Government's budget initiative which will literally be taking candy from the mouths of babies.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Government Members may laugh, but I want to tell them that three years ago there was a man in Ontario who was laughing.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
His name was Frank Miller. He introduced a budget which taxed candy for babies, which taxed sanitary napkins as a non-essential item, and which taxed a cup of
The Budget-Ms. Copps
coffee. Instead of learning from the Miller lesson, the Government, under the leadership of the Prime Minister, introduced a tax on soap, shampoo, candies and pet food which in the most regressive way hits out at those families that can least afford to pay. The facts speak for themselves.
Let us look at the impact of this particular Budget. GIS recipients, that is those who are in the worst position of poverty in the country, will see their own purchasing power, as little as it is, and their own income reduced by 33 per cent by the end of this decade. They will see a 33 per cent reduction in their purchasing power. In the first full year that this insidious Budget will take effect, $2.4 billion will be taken directly from the pockets of those consumers who pump money back into the economy by buying chocolate bars-heaven forbid that they should be allowed to have a chocolate bar-coffee and pet food, items which ordinary Canadians pay for on a daily and weekly basis.
This Budget is not a fair one. It cushions the rich and it says that a Canadian family of four earning $15,000 per year, which is not the lap of luxury, will be paying 36 per cent more in taxes in 1990, while a family of four earning $200,000 per year will be paying 2 per cent more in taxes. Where is the fairness in asking a family of four earning $15,000 to pay 36 per cent more in taxes at the same time as saying to a family earning $200,000 that its tax burden will be increased by 2 per cent? If we take into consideration the $125,000 cash bonus to the rich, we discover that the typical family of four earning $15,000 will be paying $413 more in taxes and the family earning $200,000 as a result of this cash bonus, this cash for life bonanza, will be paying $2,352 less in taxes than they paid before the Budget was introduced. The cash for life lottery does not only benefit people who buy tickets; the Government has given a $125,000 cash write-off to the rich. Is it fair to ask a $15,000 per year family to pay more and to give a tax break which will result in savings of more than $2,000 to a family earning $200,000?
I represent the most industrialized riding in Hamilton, the great riding of Hamilton East.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, no.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If the Hon. Member would like to check the figures, he can look at the latest census. Then he will be aware of the fact that the people in my riding are steelworkers; they are construction workers. Many of them are working for the minimum wage. In particular, women are working for 63 cents of every dollar earned by men. Many of those people voted for the Conservative Party because they believed the message of fairness preached by the Prime Minister. They actually believed the Prime Minister when he said that he would not touch the pensions of senior citizens. In fact, he said it right here in the House last December.
If government Members had a modicum of integrity, they would rise in their places today and dissociate themselves from this vicious attack on the pensions of senior citizens, senior citizens who are living below the minimum wage. Also, they believed the Prime Minister when he said he would reach out

May 30, 1985
The Budget-Ms. Copps
to try to develop employment equity for women. What do we see for women in the Budget? For the women of the country we see absolutely nothing, absolutely no budgetary provisions for the introduction of employment equity into the federal Public Service. On the contrary, we see by the Government's own secret Cabinet documents that it is expecting to garner a savings of almost half a billion dollars as a direct result of Public Service rationalization.
We have heard government Members speak about rationalization and say how tremendous it is that the Government will be saving almost half a billion dollars. However, rationalization means that those women currently employed in ghettoized jobs in the Public Service, those women in private companies who are currently under federal labour law that does not respect the concept of equal pay for work of equal value, will be further reduced because the federal Government has made absolutely no provision to implement the kind of employment equity which the Prime Minister promised when he spoke to the women of Canada. If we look at the figures, we discover that rationalization in federal Public Service terms means dumping those women who currently occupy the lowest rungs of employment within the federal Government. It is anticipated that more than 60 per cent of those directly affected by rationalization will be women. They will also happen to be those women who are currently at the lowest end of the federal salary scale. Last August the Prime Minister went before the women of Canada and made promises-

-that as soon as he was elected on September 4, he would start fighting to ensure that Canadian women would get equal pay for work of equal value. And now we see what happened. The Prime Minister and his Minister of Finance got together to figure out how to take money from the middle class, from Canadian women and from the elderly and hand it over to their own Progressive Conservative friends. The real meaning, the true spirit of the Progressive Conservative Party has come through in this Budget, Mr. Speaker, because it is clear to see that the Prime Minister has decided to give a bonus of $125,000 to families already earning more than $200,000, while at the same time taking money out of the pockets of families earning less than $15,000... they are going to be paying over $400 in taxes. Mr. Speaker, in addition to taking $400 out of the pockets of lower income families, they also felt they had to take money from the elderly poor in Canada.
When I have a chance to talk to senior citizens in my riding,
I find that of course they would like to work together will all Canadians to create jobs, but Mr. Speaker, it is not fair to ask our own elderly people who are already living below the poverty line to give up 3 per cent of their benefits next year and 3 per cent the year after. By the time we get to the end of the period covered by this Budget, in 1990, the elderly will have lost more than 30 per cent of their purchasing power because of these budget cuts.
Mr. Speaker, it is not just the people who are already getting other pensions. Most of these people, 600,000 to be exact, are already living below the poverty line. And at the same time, the Minister of Finance comes up with some of the most extraordinary measures for the benefit of private companies and wealthier Canadians who can use retirement savings as a tax shelter. I think that this Budget, which for the first time has really shown the true colours of conservatism in Canada, has broken promises that were made to the Canadian poeple and betrayed hopes that were raised, after September 4, before the Budget was announced.
Mr. Speaker, about employment: this Budget does not contain a single measure that will directly create jobs for young Canadian men and women. There is not a single measure that will provide for this, because the Minister of Finance has washed his hands like Pontius Pilate by saying that the private sector is going to take care of everything for Canadian men and women. I beg the Prime Minister and I beg the Minister of Finance to at least do three things: First, to re-index fully all pensions and especially those of Canadians living below the poverty line. Second, to introduce measures that will directly create jobs for ridings such as Hamilton East where the unemployment rate is already over 11 per cent. And third, to give Canadians the assurance that the next Budget this Minister and this Government will bring down will bear the hallmark of equality and that the middle class will not bear the brunt of cutbacks while the pockets of the wealthiest in Canada are being filled.
That, Mr. Speaker, is conservative philosophy. I beg the Minister of Finance to turn away from the policy of conservatism, from this policy for the rich, and to remember that Canadians elected him to represent the middle class and all Canadians on September 4, and to act accordingly.

That is the Conservative philosophy that we will see unfold over the next four years. It is the philosophy which we in the Liberal Party will fight, and fight hard, on behalf of middle-income, ordinary and poor Canadians.
