speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am starting to feel like someone who has to apologize for the mess that was created over the last 20 years, left to us by the Liberal Party. Believe me, 1 do not want to stand here and apologize to anyone in this country.
1 visited every nursing home and every senior citizens' home in the constituency of Saskatoon East during the last election campaign. The least selfish of the entire electorate were the senior citizens of that constituency who never once asked for more for themselves, but asked for more for the youth of this country. It seems to me that more than anything else, the Budget has youth, jobs and promise for the future written all over it.
I would like to ask the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps), who I think is using scare tactics in her presentation, if she can give me specific calculations for her figures indicating that there will be a tax increase of 30 per cent for a typical family earning $15,000 per year and a tax increase of 2 per cent for the typical family earning $200,000 per year. I would like to see some item-by-item calculations for that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, unlike the Hon. Member, I have had the opportunity of reading the Budget. Those figures are drawn directly from the budget documents, directly from the Minister's own assessments and directly from the Government's decision to increase taxes, hidden and direct, on the middle class and in particular on senior citizens, and to in fact give a tax holiday to the same people on whom the Government promised to impose a minimum tax.
I am getting tired of the typical Conservative palaver on this particular subject. Conservative members seem to suggest that because senior citizens who are now living below the poverty line do not want to see a further reduction in their Guaranteed Income Supplements and their Old Age Security, they are being selfish. I am here for the future too. I want jobs for my brother, my sister, my children, my family and my grandchildren. However, I do not want those jobs to be delivered at the expense of those people who have built this country over the last 60 years.
The majority of those people living in poverty, as everyone in the House knows, are women who did not have the opportunity to accrue pension credits because they were not working outside the home. They are those people who have outlived their husbands and whose benefits from where their husbands worked have been cut or perhaps never existed. Those are the people whose pockets this Government is reaching out to pick of $30 per month. Perhaps $30 per month is not a lot to the Minister of Finance. Perhaps $30 per month is not a lot to the Hon. Member for Saskatoon East (Mr. Ravis). However, $30 per month is a lot for those seniors, and particularly women,
who are being robbed by this Budget, which is a vicious attack on the seniors of this country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to deal briefly with some of the concerns that exist in the country and then deal with the rationale behind the change in the tax system as regards capital gains. This last year, the debt of our country in relation to our Gross National Product reached 5.3 per cent of GNP, the highest level by far in the history of the country. That percentage is higher than it was during the Great Depression and higher than it was at any time during the war. It is a debt burden that was saddled on the country by administrations run by the now Official Opposition, administrations that created a horror show not only for us but for our children, our grandchildren and our grandchildren yet to come.
To hear the wailing, weeping, gnashing of teeth and nonsense that is coming from the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) makes me sick. Her speech was a misrepresentation right from beginning to end. Through this Budget, we have protected senior citizens who need assistance. We have protected them with the Guaranteed Income Supplement, which will be increased and will look after any pension deficiency. The Hon. Member for Hamilton East knows that, but she is making misrepresentation after misrepresentation because that is all she knows how to do.
Let us deal with the financial position of the country. Last year it was necessary for us to go to the markets to borrow $30 billion. This year we will have to borrow only $28 billion. Through this Budget, we have managed to cut back our borrowing requirements by $2 billion. More than that, in the national accounts, we showed a deficit last year of $31.1 billion. That has been reduced to $27.5 billion. There has been a reduction of $3.6 billion in our national deficit. The deficit is down $3.6 billion in cash over the year ending March 31. I suspect it has gone down even more than that.
If you look, Mr. Speaker, at the calculations for interest made in the November 8 statement, you will note that interest calculations then were less than they are forecast to be in this Budget. Strangely enough, since we were elected in September, interest rates have dropped almost 3 per cent. I suggest that as long as we are fortunate enough to be able to continue to drive interest rates down, we will be able to carry the national debt more reasonably, and it may well be possible for us to reduce the deficit by $5 billion. That is an important consideration when taking into account the problems faced by young people, businesses and home owners when trying to make our country grow.
As has been pointed out earlier today, we cannot put people to work when interest rates are at 22 per cent. That is what we got from the Trudeau Government. It is important to take a look at where we are going. Bit by bit, through this Budget and with our change in philosophy, we are going to be able to turn things around and will eventually be able to whittle away at our enormous, suffocating, totally encumbering national debt.
May 30, 1985

A number of people have indicated that we were being a bit unfair by implementing capital gains tax relief. I would like to read into the record a memo I sent to my colleagues regarding the proposed Budget prior to the bringing down of the Budget. The memo is dated March 21, 1985. I had an opportunity to analyse the returns to the country from the taxation of capital gains. Total capital gains in 1982, the last year for which figures are available, were $1.6 billion. Against those taxable gains, the deductible losses were $240 million. The actual losses were $700 million, but as you know, Mr. Speaker, under the current capital gains law, one cannot deduct all one's losses, so taxpayers were able to deduct only $240 million. Therefore, capital gains subject to tax amounted to $1.36 billion. With that background information in mind, my memo reads:
Bearing in mind that the total taxable income in 1982, up substantially from 1981, was $158.3 billion. Taxable capital gains net from deductible capital losses represents significantly less than 1 per cent of taxable income.
If one assumes that both federal and provincial taxes are averaging no more than 35 per cent-this is undoubtedly high-the maximum collected both federally and provincially inclusive is $476 million.
Those from the Finance Department might say that this was a bad year for capital gains receipts. Clearly, it was not a bad year for other income receipts. Indeed, Table 1 clearly shows the progression of tax receipts. In 1982, the over-all taxable income grew by nearly $24 billion.
May I suggest, Sir, that when we talk about abolishing capital gains, it does not mean, that much revenue will be lost. Indeed, those who claim we are losing revenue, are wrong. The revenue loss in fact is negligible. That brings me to the question of what the Budget says. There is a provision for $300 million as a tax expenditure this year for capital gains relief and $600 million next year for capital gains relief. I suggest that the budget figures are out by at least ten times. I think that we in this House ought to have an opportunity-and we certainly will when Ways and Means motions are presented to us in the Finance Committee-to cross-examine the officials of the Department of Finance. In that respect, may I remind you, Sir, that earlier this year the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs had the opportunity to look into the whole question of capital gains taxes, particularly how they affect farmers. In that respect, the committee had before it officials from the Department of Finance. Those officials indicated that in the last year of reporting-that is the statistics for 1982-the total amount collected both corporately and personally, both by the provinces and by the federal Government, everywhere capital gains tax is collected, in any manner, anywhere, any time, was less than $1 billion.
How much real tax relief are we getting on capital gains? The figures indicate that it is pretty negligible. But it is not the relief which matters. It is the enthusiasm that capital gains relief brings to the whole community. I might point out, Sir, before I continue, that the committee report, you will recall, Mr. Speaker, recommended in recommendation No. 7 the total abolition of capital gains. The report said that "the Minister of Finance should consider the advisability of abolishing the taxation of capital gains in general". The committee's
The Budget-Mr. Blenkarn
report was a unanimous report. May I point out to you, Sir, that representing the Official Opposition was the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) and the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster). Representing the New Democratic Party was the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse) and the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo). The unanimous recommendation of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs was that there be a total abolition of capital gains taxes, and when we hear members of the Opposition standing in their place and telling us that somehow there is something wrong with what we have done, may I just tell them that the committee report was tabled in this House on April 1-and that is not long ago-and that that was the position on April 1 of the delegated Members from the Liberal Party and from the New Democratic Party. To suggest for one moment that what we have done in this Budget with respect to capital gains tax is in any way not the opinion of this House is a misrepresentation of the worst kind.
The committee went on to recommend, if you will recall, that if it was not financially possible to do something in terms of the total abolition of capital gains tax, consideration ought to be given to a once in a lifetime exemption to farmers of a capital gain of up to $400,000 on farm land. The Minister of Finance, in his wisdom, saw the importance of that recommendation and said that $500,000 was appropriate. Indeed, this Budget allows for the immediate recognition of a capital gain tax exemption of up to a $500,000 with respect to farm land. It allows businesses, and particularly small businesses to which an exemption from capital gains tax is so important, to be able to benefit equally from the incentive which this capital gains tax assistance creates.
I would like now to go into the theory behind the removal of capital gains tax. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that there is a vast difference between capital and income. Capital is something which we have acquired. Income is something which we have acquired. Income is something we earn when we do something in the nature of an adventure in trade. Capital is something we own. There really is only one form of capital which does not depreciate in the long run. A business or a building may go up in value because it is temporarily in a place where people want to rent it or own it. And some paintings, because of a shortage or the particular quality of a painting, may go up in value. But, generally speaking, everything created by man eventually becomes dust, and that includes buildings, cars, machinery, furniture and paintings. Indeed, everything ever created by man eventually becomes dust. Chattels, goods and things do not rise in value except by inflation and except if they specifically happen to be scarce, and then only for a short while.
The only thing that is permanently scarce in this world is land. It, of course, goes up in value as the number of people in the world increases along with the desire to own land, and because the land on this earth cannot be increased in amount. So land is the kind of capital which should be taxed, and we do tax capital in land. Every municipality in this country taxes capital on land on its assessed value. Every province makes

May 30, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Blenkarn
sure that land is taxed on its assessed value. We tax land on its assessed value not for the protection of the land but to do all sorts of things. The other day I received a tax bill on some farm property I own. About $400 of the $2,800 bill was for municipal services which would help the land. The other $2,400 was for schools. The land does not send anyone to school.
We have a tax on land because that is a proper capital tax. But there is no justification for capital taxes on other forms of capital. Since we have a tax on capital in land of 1 per cent or 2 per cent of the value of that land annually, surely to goodness, in the interests of justice, we have already affected those who own land. Therefore, there is really no justification for any tax on capital gains except, perhaps, that sometimes we allow people in the organization of their affairs to treat what should be income as capital.
May I point out to you, Sir, the situation of a grocer who happens to buy and sell oranges. There is no question that if he buys oranges by the crate and sells them by the dozen, it is a transaction in the nature of trade. Obviously the grocer is taxable on the profit on the oranges. Is there any reason why those who trade in stocks, houses, boats, cars, planes or whatever should not be taxed as traders? I say there is not. That is in the nature of trade and it should never be treated as a capital gain. Unfortunately, under our existing law it has been treated that way. Therefore, I propose that the Minister, when he is organizing his regulations and statutes to define what is income and what is capital gain, perhaps think about using the time test.
The suggestion I have made to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), and I intend to continue making it, is that when capital assets are sold before the end of the five year period that it be up to the taxpayer to prove it was really a capital gain. If you sell your house within a five-year period, you had better justify it; buying a bigger house or moving to another city, or something of that nature, not just turning it over to make a quick buck. On the other hand, after five years, it should be up to the Government to show that the transaction was in the nature of trade. I do not think there would be any problem with that. Most of these things are self-evident. It is important, if we are going to be fair, to make sure that transactions in the nature of trade not be disguised as capital gains. That is not the point of the removal of the capital gains tax.
Sir, removal of the capital gains tax will probably do more than any other measure to stimulate our economy. On the day of the budget speech I had an opportunity to slip out and chat briefly with a commentator from the CBC. He said that here is the day to do it, here is the day to go down to Cape Breton and start a new business. It will be tax free and look at the gain you can make. It is all tax free. Isn't that an incentive to do something? I said I had not thought of it, but maybe he and I ought to go down there together. But I say to you, Sir, that the opportunity to make a gain will encourage investment and
create jobs. That is what we are here to do. The Province of Ontario was very anti-gambling for a long time, and then it got into lotteries. Lottery ticket sales today are several times in excess of the total betting on horse racing. Canadians are not afraid to invest; they want to take a chance, they want to buy something they think will give them a return of some kind. They want the sizzle and the go that tax-free capital gains will give them. They will put their money into venture after venture, and it is those ventures that will put our people back to work.
In reorganizing the capital system of our companies, it is essential that we have more money invested through equity and less through debt. One of the problems Canadian corporations face is that they are up to their ears in mortgages. What we offer here with capital gains tax relief is an incentive to corporations and businesses generally to issue more equity. This is because dividends are still taxed, and there is then an incentive for companies to plough their profits back into the treasury and build their equity even further. As long as the shares in the company can be traded, the retained earnings in effect create a larger share value, and that value can be realized tax free if capital gains taxes are removed. That fact alone will enable all sorts of investment to take place which would not otherwise be the case. It is that new investment that will change this country around. We cannot go on any longer the way we have. We must have a new way, and that new way is the way of free enterprise, and capital gains tax removal makes that possible.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Budget we are addressing today, the first Conservative Budget, is very clever, very cunning and very diabolical. There is much coming and going, pushing and shoving, pluses and minuses. There is a lot of shuffling about in this Budget, and I think it is so in order to confuse people. It is to give the appearance of something being done about everything. Then the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) can say to the poor people that there is going to be a minimum tax on the rich. Unfortunately, the date and amount are unspecified. But the taxes, which affect all Canadians, and disproportionately affect poor Canadians because they spend more of their money on goods and services, start immediately, and the excise taxes start promptly. There is going to be a large tax on corporations. However, it is only for the short term. Yet the other taxes, the partial deindexing, the excise taxes, increased personal income taxes, all start immediately and continue indefinitely. There is going to be a $500,000 capital gains exemption, a new tax holiday and a shameful one.
Over the long term we can see that the slide which the Liberals started and which has been going on for a couple of decades is now being accelerated by the Conservatives, higher taxes on individuals, lower taxes on corporations. The estimates are that by 1990-91 there will be an increase of $4.1 billion in personal income tax, $2.6 billion in sales tax, and a reduction of $2.2 billion in taxes for corporations.
Lower and middle-income Canadians may be relieved that
the Minister of Finance did not go on to eliminate or substan-
May 30, 1985

tially cut the old age pension and family allowance, but what we have here is much sneakier. It is an erosion. The amount being cut this year is not large, although it is still going to hurt a number of people. But the effect is cumulative. It goes on and on and on, year after year. Families are going to be paying more, their family allowance is going to be less. A person who is 50 years old now will receive $1,500 less by the time he or she retires 15 years from now than they would have prior to this Budget. A hundred dollars a year does not sound like very much, although it is a lot for some people, but it adds up year after year after and means that people who cannot afford it are going to be forced to pay more and a large number of people are going to be badly hurt.
Perhaps it is as important to comment on what is not in this Budget as what there is, that is, tax reform. We simply do not have tax equity here, and the kind of tax reform that the NDP raised throughout the election campaign and on which we got at least some positive response simply cannot be seen here. We see a surtax, a temporary one on high incomes, but note that 5 per cent of zero is still zero. If the loopholes which allow so many people in high income brackets to pay no taxes at all are not closed, this surtax is meaningless. It is, in fact, another incentive to use those loopholes.
All of these benefits for corporations and richer individuals are not tied to job creation. There is a notion of the trickle down theory in this Budget. That is, if you throw buckets of money at the big corporations and wealthier individuals, they will do something with the money and a certain amount of it will trickle down into job creation, some of it staying in the country. Undoubtedly some of it will trickle down in Canada and create jobs, but how much? Is this a responsible way in which to use the taxpayer's money? Taxes are collected from all Canadians, although disproportionately from lower and middle-income Canadians. Yet, they are being redistributed to those who are better off with the vain hope that some of it will come back. This is an irresponsible and immoral way to use the taxpayers' money.
In the fine print of the Budget there are provisions that up to 31 per cent of pension funds can now be put into foreign investments, whereas previously only 10 per cent could be so invested. Up to $28 billion of the $90 billion in pension funds currently being held in Canada could go into foreign investment. What will that do for job creation in Canada?
This is not a jobs Budget, nor is it one that will reduce the deficit. Although there is much talk about reducing the deficit, in fact this Budget only reduces the increase in the deficit. It is not an absolute decrease in the deficit which will continue to accumulate. The deficit will not decrease until Canadians are put back to work and are earning incomes and paying taxes rather than collecting unemployment insurance. The Minister of Finance had to admit that his own figures of last fall overestimated the revenues that would be generated. I expect he will find that he continues to be overly optimistic because the revenues will not come in while we have high unemploy-
The Budget-Ms. McDonald
ment and we will not get unemployment down when the priority is this fixation with the deficit rather than with job creation itself.
This is not a fair Budget, but is it tough? Unfortunately, it is for some people. It is certainly tough for those who will lose jobs directly through reductions in the Public Service and for those who will lose jobs indirectly, particularly in small businesses because purchasing power is going to be reduced by this Budget. The increase of sales tax and income tax along with the reduction in family allowance and old age pensions means that people will have less money to spend. Therefore, small companies which are at the margin will not get enough business. Estimates are that 50,000 people the year and 100,000 next year will lose their jobs as a result of the decline in purchasing power.
This is also a tough Budget for those concerned about international development. It is shameful that a country as rich as Canada should withdraw $50 million from official international development assistance. By digging into their pockets for famine relief Canadians showed that they cared. Yet an amount comparable to what they gave is being withdrawn by the Government from international development. There is no incentive or encouragement for Canadians to give generously when the Government is cutting back on its development assistance. Maurice Strong, a noted international expert on development aid, has stressed the need for international development now. The emergency is not over. Unless there is aid for development purposes, famine will continue. We must help to build self-sufficiency in these countries. This reduction in aid is a heartless measure.
This Budget is tough on pensioners. The President of the National Anti-Poverty Organisation has stressed the hardships that this will cause. To the financially secure, $100 a year does not sound like much, but to the elderly poor, any erosion of purchasing power cuts into life's necessities. It will increase poverty in the most vulnerable people, senior citizens, who will not be able to go out and find other sources of income. It is again the sneaky cumulative effect. It is not much now, but it is adding up.
The President of the Ontario Federation of Labour spoke about the heartlessness, futility and foolishness of this Budget. He said that it is not that the deficit is no problem, because it is, but it is not the only problem or even the most pressing. This Budget will, in the long run, end up boosting instead of cutting the debt. If the Government were serious about reducing the deficit it would reduce both unemployment and interest rates, two of the heaviest contributors to the national debt.
The capital gains tax exemption is one of the most flagrant parts of this Budget. It is an outrageous example of the Conservative Government's priorities. It is a $500,000 giveaway which will overwhelmingly go to the top 1 per cent of income earners. Canada is already very generous on capital gains. They were taxed at only half the rate of other income. When the Carter Commission on taxation recommended in 1967 that capital gains be taxed at the same rate as other income, there was a tremendous outcry from the financial

May 30, 1985
The Budget-Ms. McDonald
community. That recommendation was successfully brought down and halved. A compromise was made and capital gains were taxed at only half the rate.
This matter has been explored over the years. A Department of Finance study in 1980 pointed out that Canada taxes capital gains at a lower rate than do other industrialized countries. The study concludes that even full elimination of capital gains could not be expected to have any noticeable impact on total investment. The idea that this giveaway to the rich will result in more jobs and greater investment is belied by studies of the Department of Finance itself. Other countries with economies at least as successful as ours and with lower rates of unemployment have higher rates of capital gains taxation.
There is an impact on fairness, if not on stimulating the economy. The exemption of capital gains tax would leave Canada as the only industrialized country which permitted large amounts of wealth to be accumulated and passed through generations without any tax liability. Five hundred individuals with incomes of over $100,000 derive almost all of their income from capital gains. This is flagrantly unfair, and in the last election campaign the Conservatives promised to address it. Instead, they will continue the tax holiday for these people.
Let us now consider arts and culture.
[ Translation]
I was looking forward to some provision in the Budget which would make life easier for the artistic community, not as a result of promises made by the Conservatives during the election campaign-they broke them all-but because of the strong opposition expressed by artists when budget cut-backs were announced in the November economic statement.
Admittedly, their protests were not a total loss-arts and culture are mentioned with some deference in this Budget.
There are even two tax reform proposals, but they concern unfortunately very few people. The purpose of the first one is to rectify a fiscal aberration which caused works of art to be treated just as manufactured goods for income tax purposes. It was scandalous. Artist Tony Onley had even threatened to burn his works on a beach in Vancouver. Thanks to this budget, Mr. Onley can now put away his matches and his works have been saved from destruction.
The second proposal will make it possible for artists to have deductible artistic donations just as we have deductible charitable donations. The artistic community are being asked to continue being the patrons of the arts. Although Canadian artists make up probably the least remunerated occupational group in this country, the government wants them to continue working without pay. We, on the contrary, were hoping for initiatives to raise their incomes and give them the protection of our social programs, such as Unemployment Insurance benefits and Pension Plans.
Well, the Sub-Committee on the Taxation of Visual and
Performing Artists and Writers had put forward during the
last Parliament 31 recommendations aimed at reducing the tax burden of Canadian artists. These recommendations had been supported by Progressive Conservative Party members while in the opposition. Now that they have an opportunity to follow up on those proposals, they have shelved the major recommendations.
This Budget contains nothing for musicians. Yet, the subcommittee recommended that all their expenses be deductible and that they be deemed to be self-employed because of the high expenses incurred in that profession.
Still nothing for the writers in spite of recommendations that their expenses for research and writing purposes be deductible.
Another recommendation that grants be considered as business income was ignored. This recommendation would have authorized the larger deductions which are absolutely necessary for people with a low income and substantial expenses.
For a performing artist, still nothing, neither for the deduction of expenses nor for their inclusion under the Unemployment Insurance Plan. Yet, these artists are often unemployed for rather long periods without being eligible for benefits, which would not be so bad if they were better paid, but they are not.
The third Budget proposal related to artists is that a task force be established to develop incentives for the private sector to support the arts. No one can be against measures to increase support for the arts, but the difficulties must be pointed out. First, such measures must not replace existing Government support. The Government even promised during the election campaign that its financial support would be increased according to the increase in the cost of living. These other incentives should be over and above Government support. Unfortunately, the present Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse) does not seem to be aware of those promises. He is banking on the possibility of an increase in private sector donations to justify the budgetary cut-backs. Obviously, a task force to look into a certain problem is not the answer. A task force does not put bread on the table.
The culture cut-backs are extremely disturbing. Since these are not new cut-backs in the Budget, the arts and culture community breathed a sigh of relief. However, the cut-backs continue and, for the first time in history, the Canada Council has less money to spend this year than the previous year. Although it suffered from inadequate increases in the past, it faces real hardship from a reduction.
The Budget is a severe disappointment for women. A number of promises were made to women in the course of the election campaign, including child care, credit arrangements and job training. These promises have not been fulfilled. The few measures that have been taken with respect to pensions for
May 30, 1985

women are woefully inadequate. While I am pleased that there is an end to discrimination on annuities, I point out that this had been recommended as far back as 1970 by the Royal Commission on the Status of Women in Canada. Until the Canada Pension Plan is improved and women can take part in that plan and receive adequate pensions, women will face difficulties with pensions. It is not enough merely to improve pensions in the private sector because half the women in the labour force do not benefit from pensions in the private sector.
These reforms are welcome only to those who are better off. They do not address the problems facing the vast majority of Canadians.
Let me conclude by simply pointing out the futility of the Budget. It will not reduce the deficit or create jobs. Small business will be adversely affected as a result of the loss of demand. We recommended a very different approach to get people back to work and make communities economically active again.
It is fundamentally a dishonest Budget and pretends to be what it is not. The Minister uses a combination of threat and fraud; threat that unless people bite the bullet there will be even more jobs to lose, and fraud that the rich have to be bought off by even greater giveaways to provide even a small number of jobs.
There is the illusion of fairness because some minor measures have been implemented. They are overturned by the more serious matters, which means that the rich will profit from this Budget while low and middle-income Canadians will be badly hurt.
We are seeing a massive redistribution of income in this country. It is being done in a sneaky manner, gradually, year by year. It represents a very serious betrayal of the Conservative election promises. It is a sad day when we see the true colours of the Conservative Party. I hope the population of Canada will not be fooled by the shuffling and will see where this Budget is really taking Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

Mr. Speaker, will the Hon. Member explain to the House how she can rationalize her position in saying that this is an anti-small business Budget? All of the organizations representing small businesses herald the Budget as a very positive one for the small business sector, which is really one of the main engines of growth and economic opportunity in this country.
With respect to the application of the capital gains tax exemption, contrary to the Hon. Member's suggestion that it is a boon to the rich, it is considered in most corners as an excellent incentive to encourage individual entrepreneurs and families to engage in small business activites. It would be very similar to the family farm enterprise where families work together to create an investment in land, machinery and equipment that will become a retirement fund in later years.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a Budget that reduces purchasing power as significantly as does this Budget will be very harmful for small business which depends on the purchase of
The Budget-Ms. McDonald
goods and services. The Budget takes money from the hands of families who buy food, services and other necessities.
The Budget is reducing the family allowance and old age pension while increasing taxes. This means that people will have less money to spend. How can businesses be pleased that their customers will not have as much money to spend on their businesses? I suggest it will hurt businesses.
How will people increase their purchases? The unemployed will not be making large purchases and the Budget will not reduce unemployment. There will be direct lay-offs as a result of the Budget and indirect lay-offs as small businesses are hurt by it. A Budget that reduces the purchasing power reduces business.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am not sure what experience the Hon. Member has in running a small business, but when all the leading spokesmen for the small business sector in this country have heralded the Budget as very positive, particularly as it relates to the small business sector, how can the Hon. Member stand in the House and argue against it? What rationale can she use to challenge the statements of the respresentatives of the small business sector in this country?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Minister has simply not addressed the point in question, which is, how do people become customers if they do not have money in their pockets with which to buy? If you reduce purchasing power, what are people going to spend? If people do not have money, how are they going to spend it? The Minister has not answered how people are going to spend money they do not have.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, perhaps the Hon. Member could answer this question: is she saying that the small business sector is not happy with the Budget? Or is she saying that it is happy with the Budget but the small business sector does not know what it is talking about, that it is ignorant in its assessment?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am simply pointing out one of the unhappy facts of life, that reducing purchasing power is going to hurt. I think small business will be very seriously hurt. The proof of the pudding is in the eating. Let us talk about it a year from now and see who is right, the Member or I.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to express appreciation for the Hon. Member's remarks-

speechtext:
-expressing her concerns. I think we have all listened with benefit. 1 would like to thank her for the tone in which she expressed her views. She avoided some of the fabricated passion that many of her colleagues have demonstrated when speaking on the same subject.
However, I have to take issue with the Hon. Member on some of the substance of her address. I will take time, Mr. Speaker, to refer only to her references to the capital gains provision in the Budget, namely referring to it as a $500,000 giveaway. Where is the giveaway of half a million dollars? This would imply to someone who did not understand this Budget or did not understand the system of capital gains
beforehand that somehow $500,000 would actually be given away.
We know, as the Hon. Member for Broadview Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) unintentionally admitted a few sentences later in the address, that the capital gains tax is imposed on only half of the capital gains to start with. We are now talking about a tax on $250,000 not $500,000. When we get down to the $250,000, it is not $250,000 that will be made this year because the provision involves a progressive initiation of the introduction of the capital gains tax exemption. What will we have this year? We will have exemption on only $20,000 in capital gains, namely, the tax that would be imposed on $10,000 of capital gains. Where is this half a million dollar giveaway which the Hon. Member is talking about? 1 think this is alarming people. I agree that, unintentionally, there has been a kind of scare tactic used. I would say unintentionally. Nonetheless it is a scare tactic that somehow this Government is giving the rich another half a million dollars when in fact we are offering an incentive for investors to do exactly what the Hon. Member should want, and I believe does want.
We have mentioned family farms and family businesses. What we are doing is trying to accomplish the objective which the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) indicated, namely the need of private business to raise more capital through equity investment rather than going into debt. Small business needs that kind of assistance. I can take the Hon. Member to a constituent, the operator of a small business, who needs to expand, who is afraid to undertake more debt even at today's interest rates, but who would like to sell equity capital in his business. This provision will encourage individual investors and the Budget will encourage pension funds and other sources of capital supply. Just a half hour before listening to the Hon. Member I talked to an associate in Metro Toronto who told me that already pension funds are making provisions to enlarge portfolios through investment in small businesses. My friend in Scarborough will benefit.

Let me also point out, with regard to the Member's second point, that the incentive to invest in small business for pension funds permits investment in foreign companies. We have, on the one hand, a good measure to encourage and invest in small businesses in Canada-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
