subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to take part in this budget debate. For me it is a double pleasure because I am making my maiden speech in this historic Chamber.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Budget brought down on May 23 by the Hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is a continuation of the direction set out in his November 8, 1984, economic statement. It is a very clear signal to the Canadian people that we are a responsible Government and that we are prepared to make the tough economic decisions which are required to govern.
It is just over one year ago that 1 was seeking the nomination in my constituency and later fighting the election campaign. The clear message given to me by the people of my constituency was "give us less government. Stop forcing things on us like metrication and introducing new Crown corporations to compete with the private sector. Instead, get the economy moving". The Minister's budget will do just that. In addition, it will start to control that monster, the federal deficit.
I would like to thank the constituents of the Moose Jaw federal constituency for doing me the great honour of electing me as their Member of Parliament. I would also like to assure my constituents that it is an honour I do not take lightly, and I will continue to represent their concerns to the very best of my ability.
I should like to pay tribute to the former Hon. Member for Moose Jaw, Mr. Doug Neil. Mr. Neil was a Member of the House from 1972 until the last election. He served his constituency and Canada well during that time. This was particularly evident in the area of rail line abandonment and in his publication known as the Neil report. Many of the recommendations made in the report were adopted by the previous Government and will continue to serve as a guide in this vital area for some time to come.
The Moose Jaw federal constituency is located in south central Saskatchewan and is made up of people of all racial extractions and a wide variety of ethnic origins. While English is the mother tongue of most of the residents, we have people of other nationalities who are also keeping their cultures alive through their own groups. We have people from the British Isles, from many European countries such as the Ukraine, Germany, Russia and Poland and from Scandivanian and oriental countries. Many of these people are descendants of the original settlers who came to Canada seeking land and freedom. They were hardy individuals who adapted to the harsh environment and prospered. By helping each other, these
The Budget-Mr. Gottselig
people built the towns and cities and laid the framework of rural Saskatchewan as we know it today.
Moose Jaw is the focal point of the riding. It was known for many years as the friendly city. However, it has more recently been referred to as the band capital of North America. The City of Moose Jaw was incorporated in 1903, and there are some very interesting legends regarding the origin of its name. One legend has it that the course taken by the Moose Jaw River resembles the jawbone of a moose. Another has it that one of the early explorers, the Earl of Mulberry, repaired his ox-cart there with the jawbone of a moose. Another myth is that the early residents, some local Indians, used to winter in that area because the weather was much warmer, and they referred to it as Moosegaw, and of course the white man changed it to Moose Jaw.
Moose Jaw is a railway divisional point on the CP Moose Jaw division. It is the largest division in the system. It has 1,873 miles of track, and last year over 75,000 loaded cars moved out of that division. Most of these were destined for Thunder Bay with grain. However, there were also cars of oil, steel and potash. CP Rail employs approximately 700 people in the City of Moose Jaw. The Saskatchewan Technical Institute in Moose Jaw has been providing training for almost 30 years. The institute offers 34 business, engineering and industrial programs to over 5,000 students. In addition, it has an extension division which delivers programs throughout the province.
CFB Moose Jaw is adjacent to this city. Over 1,200 military personnel, as well as 300 civilian employees, provide the workforce to maintain the base. It is the busiest airport in Canada with either a take off or a landing every 45 seconds. With an annual payroll of over $21 million and a further $18 million worth of purchases in the area, it contributes greatly to the economy of Moose Jaw and district. CFB Moose Jaw is also the home of the Snowbirds, Canada's aerobatic air team. They perform at the Moose Jaw Air Show as well as at many other locations in Canada and the United States. The Moose Jaw Air Show attracts over 50,000 people each year.
The constituency of Moose Jaw covers a large rural area, roughly 10,000 square miles, and has a total population of 70,000 people. It runs north from Old Wives Lake in the south, to within 30 miles from the City of Saskatoon. Much of the west boundary is made up of the mighty South Saskatchewan River and Lake Diefenbaker. The area around the City of Moose Jaw has some of the finest farm land in the west. This area is known as the Regina Plains. It is known far and wide as being a top producer of high quality bread wheat. It takes in the towns of Pense, Belle Plaine and the area south to Drink-water, Rouleau and Briercrest. West and south of Moose Jaw there are many areas of grassland where the mainstay of farmers and ranchers is beef. The Town of Caronport, west of Moose Jaw, has the Briercrest Bible College with a student enrolment of 793, most of whom reside on campus. These students come from all over Canada and the United States to take a Bible course prior to entering university and technical colleges. The east boundary runs up to Last Mountain Lake

May 30, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Gottselig
with the Town of Simpson, south through Imperial, Holdfast and down to Lumsden, to within 10 miles of the capital City of Regina. The Trans-Canada Highway borders the City of Moose Jaw. Another important highway is No. 11 which runs from Regina to Saskatoon, through towns such as Craik, Davidson, which is known as the midway town, and Hanley.
Many of these towns and villages have annual summer events such as the Davidson Kinsmen Rodeo or the Central Butte Fair. However, the most widely known event in the province is the Moose Jaw Kinsmen International Band Festival, which is the largest band festival in North America. This three-day event, held annually on the May long weekend, celebrated its thirty-sixth anniversary this year and was the biggest and best ever. From a humble beginning with 12 bands, it has grown to over 125 bands with over 7,000 competing members. In addition, there were 25 choral groups and 15 field marching competitions. Bands were in attendance from Ontario to British Columbia, as well as many from the northern states. One band was in attendance from Switzerland.
Another well-known location in my constituency is the Gardiner Dam. This is one of the largest earth filled dams in the world. It is over 200 feet in height and stretches some three miles across the South Saskatchewan Valley. The lake formed by the dam is rightly named in honour of the late Right Hon. John Diefenbaker who had the foresight to commence construction of the dam in 1958 when he was Prime Minister. It was only after many years of work and study by many groups and individuals that the project finally became a reality. Much of the credit for the construction of the dam must also be given to the late Dr. Bill Tufts who practised medicine at Outlook for many years. Throughout the dustbowl years he recognized the need for irrigation and worked tirelessly for the project until it became a reality.
To give some idea of the importance of the dam, I should like to point out that approximately one half the irrigated acreage in Saskatchewan uses water either directly from Lake Diefenbaker itself or from adjoining water supply systems. The Town of Outlook where I make my home is known as the irrigation capital of Saskatchewan. It is the approximate geographical centre of this irrigation area. Irrigation has allowed farmers to grow a wide variety of new crops and to ensure that there will always be a good supply of fodder and grain for livestock feed even in years when we have severe drought, such as the one we experienced last summer.
In addition to irrigation, the dam is an important source of power for the province and recreation for many residents of the area. There are many provincial parks and cottage developments along the shores of Lake Diefenbaker. Water is also diverted into the Qu'Appelle River system which goes to Buffalo Pound Reservoir which in turn supplies water to the cities of Moose Jaw and Regina.
We have an abundance of migratory game birds throughout the constituency as well as good populations of white tail and mule deer which provide excellent hunting each fall.
The entire area has a solid agricultural base, and the people have become accustomed to the ups and downs of a farm
economy that is influenced to such a large degree by weather. Lack of rain during the growing season is one of the most serious concerns of the residents of my constituency. We realize that we cannot control the weather. However, another concern had been growing in recent years about the uncaring federal Government. The fiscal mismanagement of the previous Liberal Government has greatly damaged the economy of Canada, and nowhere was this more evident than in the west.
The Liberal Party was unable to elect a representative from the area west of Winnipeg and, as a result, we had no one but a tired old Senator to speak for us at the decision-making level. We now have strong voices at this level as well as strong support on the back-benches. According to the media l am a back-bencher and far removed from the decision-making process. However, I do have a chance to put forth my ideas. I can assure my constituents that the Ministers of our Government listen and respond to our concerns.
We in the Conservative Party were elected to make a fundamental change in the style of government. This Budget will bring about that change in three vital areas. First, it will encourage the private initiative of individual Canadians and they, not the Government, will decide what is best. We must manage Government more effectively. We must cut waste and trim away the fat. By putting our own house in order, we will create a healthier and more effective private sector.
Finally, we must control the spiralling national debt. We all know that we cannot borrow our way out of this deficit. The Liberals tried that for too long-with disastrous results. We have only to look at our own operations, be they running a home, a farm or a business, to see that we cannot spend more than we take in. If we, as individual Canadians, spent one-third of our income to service our debt, we know only too well what the result would be.
This Budget was formulated by the Minister after the most extensive pre-budget consultations in history. We consulted with Canadians from all walks of life and from coast to coast. As a result, we have a Budget which reflects and addresses the concerns of all Canadians.
The main thrust of the Budget is to encourage the small business sector to expand and to create those permanent jobs which are required for all Canadians. The previous Government used a band-aid approach to create jobs through make-work programs-jobs that got people off the unemployment insurance rolls long enough to qualify them for unemployment insurance benefits again. That was no solution. It was a plan designed and administered by bureaucrats because the Government was bankrupt of ideas as well.
This Budget is responsible. It will be effective. Most of all, it is fair. As a Government, we have met the challenge of the 1980s head on. We have set a new course. We have reflected faith in the drive and the ingenuity of Canadians to seize the opportunities to invest in their own futures. We are saying clearly to entrepreneurial-spirited Canadians that, once more,
May 30, 1985

there will be rewards for risk taking. We will reward success rather than subsidize effort.
Last July, in Prince Albert, we promised that when we formed the Government we would remove the very unfair capital gains tax with respect to the sale of farm land. We did just that. However, we did not stop there. We also removed the capital gains tax for the small business sector in order that ordinary citizens would be free to do what they do best. We are proposing a lifetime capital gains exemption of $500,000 for individual Canadians. For farmers, this exemption will be available immediately. We have also retained the tax-free roll-over provision for farmers. We said that we would reduce the price of farm fuel. Last fall, we introduced measures to provide this reduction.
In addition to that, we dealt with other issues vital to the farm sector. For example, our Government has taken steps in the area of western grain transportation. We are in the process of removing the very unfair volume cap of 31.5 million tonnes, which acts as a disincentive to increased production. We have preserved a number of rail lines and have reopened one in Saskatchewan which had been shut down.
We have amended the Western Grain Stabilization Act in order to put badly needed funds into the hands of producers prior to the seeding of the 1985 crop. We have made important changes to the Farm Credit Corporation Act by reducing the interest rate for over 5,000 producers, as well as introducing a shared risk mortgage program. We have allowed dual labelling in order that farmers, once again, will be able to understand the directions for the proper application of farm chemicals.
We have changed the attitude of the Department of National Revenue in order that taxpayers can be treated fairly once again. We are in the process of establishing a national voluntary tripartite red meat stabilization program.
The list of our achievements goes on and on-all of this in the short space of time since we formed the Government.
Controlling the national debt is a matter of great concern to all Canadians. It is important that Canadians understand the magnitude of the deficit and debt problem and why it poses a serious threat to our ability to achieve sustained economic growth.
The public debt is simply the sum of all past deficits. It took 100 years to accumulate a debt of $18 billion. Now, less than two decades later, the debt is approaching $200 billion. This is the vicious circle in which we now find ourselves. At some point, we must begin to pay the bills for current services and not pass them on to our children.
With this Budget, and through the actions taken in November, we have reduced every area of government spending. To spread the burden of expenditure reduction fairly, the Government believes it is fair to limit the growth of transfers to provinces as well. I said limit the growth-not reduce it.
The Government can save $2 billion by the end of the decade with no absolute reduction in federal transfers. Even after this adjustment, federal transfers to provincial Govern-
The Budget-Mr. Gottselig
ments will grow significantly over the balance of this decade. In 1990-91, this would represent about the same share of total program expenditures as they do today.
I am sure we have all seen newspaper reports which state that the Government is obsessed with the deficit. That is simply not true. We are obsesed with jobs-good, satisfying and durable jobs for Canadians. The Minister of Finance said it himself. If he believed higher deficits and a rapidly rising debt would help create jobs, then he would gladly have increased the deficit. That approach has not worked in the past and it will not work now. If high deficits and high debt created employment, then there would not be one person out of work in this country.
This Budget is about equity and fairness, private initiative and enterprise, in an environment of economic, social and cultural progress. Above all, the Budget is about jobs. It realistically tackles the problems as they exist and how the Government found them on taking office last September. The Budget is not preoccupied with the deficit; instead, it recognizes the importance of controlling our debt before it ties our hands and stops us from taking the necessary steps for Canada.
The Government has taken its mandate for change and translated it into an agenda of action. We have recognized that individual initiative provides the economic strength of Canada. This Budget builds on that strength.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Questions and comments? The Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Gottselig) on his maiden speech. It was an excellent speech which outlined the issues affecting his riding. In effect, it was a report card of some of the measures this Government has taken since it was sworn into office.
The Hon. Member made reference to the issue of capital gains. I know it was a prominent issue in the election campaign. Also, I know that he debated it vigorously on the campaign trail. Given the Hon. Member's knowledge, and for the benefit of the Members of the House, could he give us his impressions of the impact the capital gains provision in this Budget will have on the farming community which he represents? In replying to the question, could he enlighten us with respect to the position taken by his NDP opponent during the election campaign, having regard to the fact that the NDP in the House has been taking such violent exception to the capital gains provision which was included in the May 23 Budget? What was the position of his NDP opponent with respect to capital gains during the course of the election campaign?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Minister of Transport for his comments. As the Minister has mentioned, the issue of capital gains was certainly an important issue raised during the election campaign. The removal of the capital gains provision will have a long-lasting effect on the West. Farmers will now be able to sell their farms without

May 30, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Gottselig
worrying about capital gains. It will mean that the generations can move as they should in transferring their land. Retiring farmers will know what they have to deal with when they sell their land.
In addition, the business sector will be able to move and thrive once again. My New Democratic Party opponent in the last federal election campaign also spoke about removing capital gains. Members of the New Democratic Party change their tunes quite often, so I suppose that that would depend on what day it is.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the statement made by the Minister was somewhat misleading. As I stated in my remarks on the Budget, this Party has always supported the removal of capital gains taxes on farms. However, we take exception to the broad scope of the legislation. We take exception to the fact that people who speculate on condominiums in Florida or on stocks can have a $500,000 tax holiday.
1 would like to ask a question of the Hon. Member. He represents the riding of Moose Jaw which is right next to my riding. I know that he is as concerned as we in Regina are about getting better water. The Hon. Member mentioned that even though he is considered a back-bencher, he does exert some influence on the decision-making process. Therefore, I wonder if the Hon. Member could enlighten us on his progress in convincing the Government that it should move immediately to help finance, along with the Conservative Government of Saskatchewan, a joint venture that would allow for the bui-dling of a pipeline from Diefenbaker Lake so that the people of Moose Jaw, Regina and the surrounding areas could have good, safe, clean water. Perhaps the Hon. Member could report to us on the progress he is making in convincing the Government, of which he is a member, to do that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the issue of a pipeline has been debated many times in Regina and Moose Jaw. There is a new water treatment plant scheduled to open fairly soon that will greatly improve the quality of water in that area. The matter of a pipeline or an open ditch will be debated for some time to come. I can assure the Hon. Member that I am certainly taking a positive stand on this and I have mentioned it and other concerns of the constituency a number of times. I am expressing the concerns of my constituents from Moose Jaw and surrounding districts and I am doing so as a member of a Government that is very responsive to the needs of the West as well as the needs of all other areas of Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am aware that the Hon. Member represents a large number of retired people who live in the City of Moose Jaw. I wonder what he will say to his retired constituents when they find out that they will be receiving approximately $100 less from their Old Age Security this year and that by 1990 a couple will receive some $1,000 less per year in Old Age Security. How will he explain that to his constituents?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the matter to which the Hon. Member refers should be put in the proper perspective. It works out to about 27 cents a day. I think that senior citizens are quite prepared to pay 27 cents a day in order to preserve what they have now and to have a country with a controlled deficit so that their grandchildren and their grandchildren's children will not have to pay that tax share.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I represent the constituency of Swift Current-Maple Creek, a constituency which shares some 55 miles of boundary with that of the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Gottselig). On behalf of my constituents I want to thank the Hon. Member for his comments. Both the Hon. Member and his constituents are very much appreciated by my constituents.
I know that the Hon. Member is a producer. He has a farm that is a going concern and, therefore, a number of the matters which were raised in the Budget are of very real concern both to the Hon. Member and to his constituents. Some concerns have been raised about the possibility of increases in fuel taxes. I wonder if the Hon. Member could enlarge on that matter from the perspective of the producer.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is talk of an increase in fuel prices effective September 3. We are going to have a reduction in the price of fuel of .7 cents per litre on June 1, and the increase on September 3 will supposedly be two cents per litre. Therefore, the net increase will be 1.3 cents. As we are moving to world prices and with the surplus on a world level, I expect that by September the price will be much lower than that because of the supply and demand situation.
I think farmers realize that they received a reduction of 4.8 cents per litre as a result of the actions taken last fall. We are going to institute this increase, if it is in fact an increase, on September 3 so that dry land farmers will have the benefit of buying fuel for this growing season at the lower price.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member will recall that he was a member of the Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs Committee and participated in the standing committee's study into tax issues in agriculture, capital gains tax with reference to agriculture, and indeed other matters. He will recall that the committee's unanimous recommendation was that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) consider the advisability of abolishing the taxation of capital gains in general. Did the Hon. Member not find that the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) and the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse), who were also members of that committee, agreed to that recommendation?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a matter of fact, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) is correct. We had all-Party representation on that committee. Although I did not attend every meeting, each meeting that I attended was attended by a member of each Party, and each member of each Party rose to say how we must eliminate capital gains tax from farm land. A unanimous recommendation came from that committee.
May 30, 1985

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But Lynn McDonald doesn't agree with that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Then she must not agree with what other members of her Party have said. 1 support fully the recommendation made by that committee. I was happy to be a part of it and to put my views forth. Once again, that indicates that the Minister has responded to our concerns. There is no doubt that this is a responsible Government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I understand as well that that committee made unanimous recommendations for an agribond issue and for changes in the taxation system as it affects part-time farmers. I wonder if the Hon. Member is also in favour of those recommendations and if he is disappointed that he did not find them in the Minister's Budget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong) for raising that point. The Minister of Finance was present at the first meeting of that committee. He told us all that he would do all of these things but that within the budget restraints with which we are faced, we may not be able to do them all at one time. He asked us to priorize the issues and to tell him which ones were number one, number two and number three. We did that. All members of that committee agreed that the single most important issue was the removal of capital gains taxes from farm land. We did that, and we gave small business people a break as well. All Canadians will now have $500,000 available to them free from capital gains taxes.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Gottselig) on his maiden speech in the House and on the way he handled himself during the question and comment period. As I recall, I don't think I was as secure on my feet. We didn't have any question and answer period when I first came to the House. That was a long time ago, as the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) will remember. But the Hon. Member did very well. I did not agree with everything he said, but he said it very well.
I would like to talk about the Budget from a different perspective. I would like to address the Budget from the point of view of the impact I see on the Atlantic area. When my colleague from Kamloops, British Columbia, spoke the other day, he talked about the trickle down theory. He said the Government was hoping that some benefits in terms of jobs and revenues would trickle down. He used the analogy of the horse. He said that if you stuff enough oats into the mouth of a horse so that it has difficulty digesting them, possibly some of the oats will trickle down for the birds at the end of the process. That was an interesting western analogy. But the analogy I like and apply to the Altantic is one originated by my colleague, Don Jamieson, a former Hon. Member of this House. That was the analogy of a new symbol for Canada, taking into account the regional realities of this country. He said that Canada really needs a new symbol. There should be a
The Budget-Mr. Rompkey
cow on the flag of Canada. She is feeding in the West, they are milking her in the centre, and we know what she is doing to us in the Atlantic provinces. That is exactly what is happening with this Budget. This Budget, as I see it, will cripple the economy of the Atlantic area. It is a crippling blow, and I say that in all sincerity from my perspective. I hope that the gentlemen on the other side of the House are listening. The main fact is-if this is a gamble on the private sector-that the private sector in the Atlantic area is not as strong as elsewhere in the country. For example, in the four provinces, close to 80 per cent of the gross provincial product is Government and 20 per cent is the private sector, as opposed to something like 35 per cent from Government in other parts of the country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am sorry, I have to leave.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am also sorry the Minister of Transport is leaving because I was hoping he would listen to this. However,
I want to tell his colleagues that the main fact to recognize is that in the Atlantic area the private sector is not as strong as elsewhere in the country. If we put all the onus on the private sector, then I think we will have a great deal of difficulty, indeed. We are very heavily dependent on fisheries, on transport and on many other government Departments. If there are cut-backs in those Departments, then we have an impact on the Atlantic area. If, at the same time, the private sector is not growing as quickly as in other parts of the country, then we will have negative growth in the Atlantic area.
Our caucus heard the other day from the Atlantic provinces economic council. It has that fear as a result of its analysis and upon talking to its members. We are going to do some computer analysis, Mr. Speaker, to see if we can determine exactly what the effect is going to be, but we are afraid that the effect on the Atlantic area is going to be negative.
For example, going back to last fall, we lost $40 million a year from the fisheries budget. Another $25 million is chopped from the fisheries by the Minister of Finance in his Budget. Those funds go to build wharves, breakwaters, haul-outs and fish plants and to put in place the facilities our fishermen need. Our provinces, as you can appreciate, Mr. Speaker, are very heavily dependent upon the fisheries. In addition to that, wharfage and dredging fees will be increased. The Budget talks about rationalization. I am afraid of that word because it translates to me into a loss of jobs and a loss of business activity.
The Government needs to have within its Budget process not only a provision for making sure that the private sector is helping this country-laudable as that objective might be- but it needs to have a concern for people and, most important of all, an understanding of regional differences. There has to be an appreciation that regions in this country are different. If a policy is brought in across the board, then it has to impact negatively on those regions which are least able to bear the burden.
For example, there is a cut in the budget of the Department
of Transport of $75 million. How is that going to be trans-

May 30, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Rompkey
lated? We don't know. We have to ask questions and we will be asking questions as to exactly what areas those cuts will affect. Will they affect CN Marine? How many boats are going to go? How many ferries are going to be lost? You can appreciate, Mr. Speaker, that the only way to get to Prince Edward Island or Newfoundland is by ferry, if one is travelling by surface. If there are changes in those coastal services in terms of boats or in terms of rates, then there will be an impact on that area. Everything we use and most of what we eat in the Atlantic area is imported from elsewhere. We are an economy which is a main customer of central Canada, and those things have an impact on us.
With respect to tourism, for example, if the gasoline tax is raised or if the price of liquor is increased, it will have, it seems to me, a generative impact on tourism which, I believe, is a sunrise industry as opposed to a sunset industry in the Altantic area. We have lost the PIP grants offshore, the grants we depended upon to do the kind of drilling which was necessary in order to determine exactly what resources were there under the sea. They will be replaced perhaps. We don't know what is to come. But we know we had them and we made use of them. We discovered and proved up the oil which was there. More drilling needs to be done. We are not yet at the end of that process. The full field of oil off the Altantic coast has not yet been discovered and we will need incentive to further prove exactly what oil is there.
I recognize that there will be no diminution of transfer payments, but there will be a reduction as compared to what they would have been by 1990 because the Minister tells us we are going to lose $2 billion. So the Atlantic provinces are not going to get as much as they would have got. They are going to get more, yes, year over year, but not as much as they would have got. There will be a net reduction in 1990.
If we go back, Mr. Speaker, to the point I made earlier, that we in the Altantic provinces are dependent on government programs and on transfer payments-like it or not, that's the reality-and if we accept that reality, then we can understand the effect that any decrease in transfer payments is going to have. For example, in the Province of Newfoundland, between 50 per cent and 60 per cent of the budget of that particular province comes from the Government of Canada. So if the economy of Newfoundland is over 80 per cent dependent on government programs, then you can see, Mr. Speaker, the effect the Budget is going to have on us.
We are going to lose 15,000 people in the civil service. Where are those jobs going to be cut? How many will be cut in the Altantic provinces? I don't know. But they will certainly add to the toll of the unemployed which is already the highest of anywhere in the country. We have close to 50 per cent unemployment among those young people who are eligible to work, and that is a tragedy. These are some of the cuts.
What else is in the Budget that will have a negative impact on the Atlantic area? The sales taxes will increase. The gasoline and aviation fuel has been increased. All of those things are going to drive up costs in the Altantic area, particularly in the North. If we consider Labrador, for example, the
only way to get in and out of there, particularly during the winter months, is by air. Already it is paying the highest air costs, not just for passengers, but for freight, of anywhere in the country. This is going to raise the costs even more. It is going to have a damaging effect on the economy in those areas. Consumers in those areas, who are already going to pay more-as will all consumers across Canada-will pay an even greater amount in areas which are rural, which are distant, and which are northern.
Then I could mention the income tax increase. So there is going to be a double whammy; a right-cross in cutting government programs, and a stiff upper cut through increased taxes. Both of these things, I believe, along with many other measures, are going to have a negative impact on the Atlantic area. Yet all the emphasis is placed and all hope is pinned on the private sector.
With regard to the transfer payments, I read in The Ottawa Citizen that the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) is undertaking a sweeping review of federal programs and is recommending other cuts and changes which are bound to make the provinces hurt. For example, the federal Government wants to leave the provision of tourism facilities solely to the private sector and the provinces, ending its partial funding under existing economic and regional development agreements. Whether that is true or not, I do not know, but the Minister of State for Tourism (Mr. McMillan) is here and maybe he can tell us whether the Government of Canada will continue with the existing policy or whether that sector will be dependent more and more on the private sector.
The article says also that the Deputy Prime Minister wants the Government to reduce subsidies for coastal shipping and ferries operated by CN Marine on the East Coast. These things worry not only me, Mr. Speaker, they worry the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie). As I pointed out, the other day he went to the Atlantic Provinces and was less than enthusiastic about this Budget. Reading from The Evening Telegram of May 25, the Minister had this to say:
Justice Minister John Crosbie says that if the federal budget has any negative effects on areas like Newfoundland, Ottawa will take measures to deal with them.
There is a direct quote which says:
If it turns out that in any of the approaches taken in this Budget there is any possibility of any damage to regionally deprived areas, then there will be changes made to deal with that-
The Minister was not going down there with a glad heart to defend the Budget. Apart from being an intelligent and witty man, the Minister of Justice is a forthright man. What he is saying here is what he knew to be correct and what I find everyone in the Atlantic Provinces knows to be correct. He went on to say, referring to the private sector:
If they can't do it, if they can't produce the jobs and the economic growth, then we won't hesitate to go in a different direction.
If they don't perform, then big brother will have to be given the job back again-
May 30, 1985

Well, there is an underlying assumption that it is not going to work in the Atlantic area. The article goes on to say the followship:
He admitted the private sector in the Atlantic area is weaker than other parts of the country and said there will have to more government support in the Atlantic region.
Crosbie said he spends a lot of his time in Ottawa ensuring that support is forthcoming.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has cut government programs and government support in that area and depends on the private sector which both I and the Minister of Justice have said is weaker than that in other parts of the country. We may not like it, but that is the reality. Nor is it just the Minister of Justice who is saying that. The St. John's Board of Trade, which is not exactly a left wing organization, says, through its President:
1 didn't see sufficient job creation activity that would do much for Newfoundland's high unemployment rate.
He said there were insufficient incentives for the housing and construction industry. He is also concerned about the phase-out of the Petroleum Incentives Program because the federal Government did not announce something to replace it. He says the board will encourage the Government to bring in other tax incentives to encourage oil companies to do exploration along the coast. Well, what about those tax incentives? The tax incentives were given to Cape Breton and maybe they should be extended elsewhere in the Atlantic Provinces, but I am not sure that the tax incentives are the right way to go because you can only get tax incentives when you start to make something. What we need in the Atlantic area, in addition to improved infrastructure, is up-front grants to start businesses going. Yes, you can bring in a multinational and if it has made profit elsewhere it can invest in the Atlantic Provinces and maybe create some jobs. But a local small firm that does not have that kind of profit, or an entrepreneur who wants to start, needs the money up-front and cannot wait until he gets his profit and tax write-downs. So I think a different approach is needed in Atlantic Canada, bearing in mind the underdeveloped infrastructure and the weakness irt the private sector.
The Community Services Council of Newfoundland says that the assumption of the federal Minister that by providing private sector incentives, everyone will join in the entrepreneurial spirit, is less likely to hold true in Newfoundland than for a manufacturing economy such as it is in Ontario. That is exactly the point I make. You cannot see all regions of the country as the same. When you have a Budget which assumes that everyone is equal, then it has a negative effect on some people. It may have a positive effect on others, sure; I believe that John Bulloch says this is good for small business. He is a credible speaker for the small business community in Canada. He represents some people in my riding as well. But I believe he was speaking nationally. He was not speaking particularly for the area I want to talk about today. The President of the Chamber of Commerce in Grand Falls, which is a rural area representing a lot of small businesses, had this to say:
The Budget-Mr. Rompkey
-Chamber members are extremely concerned that the federal Government has opted to go the route it has. that being taking such a gamble with business.
In their view the cards are stacked against this area of the nation. It is a workable formula for larger businesses and in places like Central Canada. Noted is the fact that the smaller businesses such as those to be found in Newfoundland have had to rely on Government grants-
Local business just doesn't have the wherewithal to expand and create jobs as hoped by Mr. Wilson.
Even the Premier of Newfoundland, while he said as much as he could say positively about the Budget, that it seems to represent a legitimate attempt to cope with the federal Government's financial problems and to assist economic growth through the private sector, went on to say that:
It has some negative impacts on an economy such as Newfoundland's and we will enter ongoing discussions with the federal government to ensure that proper attention is paid to overcoming regional disparities.
He is concerned about the effect any decrease in transfer payments might have. As well, he suggested that the tax increases will hurt the consumers who already have low levels of disposable income. He feels Newfoundland should be given special treatment as a province with an extremely low economic base, high unemployment and increasing cost of living.
That is the point I am making and the point I want to get across to Members on the benches opposite. You have to be flexible. In answer to my question the other day, the Minister of Finance used the word "flexibility". I encourage him to be flexible and not wait for another Budget or another four years, because we will not be able to wait. Every spokesman I have heard in the Atlantic Provinces has said the same thing. Unless changes are made, there is going to be a drastic and negative impact on our economy which we will not be able to overcome for a long, long time.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 want to congratulate the Hon. Member. As an Atlantic Canadian, I am always heartened when even a member of the Opposition marshals his considerable eloquence on behalf of the people of the Atlantic Provinces. However, I find that there is a tendency among opposition members from Newfoundland to suffer from an inverse relationship between their eloquence on the one hand and the validity of their arguments on the other. Nowhere is that more true than with respect to the Hon. Member's comments on tourism. I want to assure him now, since he invited me to do so, that his concerns with respect to the Deputy Prime Minister's task force are not founded. He can look forward to many years of active federal government involvement in subsidiary agreements under ERDA in the tourism field.
I have two questions. The first is with regard to his remarks on the alcohol tax. He mentioned, rigthly, that when federal taxes and other taxes on alcohol rise, the tourism industry is affected, usually adversely. However, the implication was that in the Budget brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) on May 23, the relevant provision on alcohol taxes would hurt the tourism industry. If it were not for the Budget, the federal excise tax on alcohol would go up 4 per cent

May 30, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Rompkey
because the relevant tax is tied to the Consumer Price Index. There is an automatic increase in the federal tax on alcohol as the CPI increases. By deindexing the federal tax on alcohol, as contemplated by the Budget, instead of that tax going up by 4 per cent this year it will be capped at only 2 per cent above the current level. Therefore, rather than hurting the tourism industry, the relevant provision will help it. Is he aware of that fact?
The Member stated that the Budget is going to slash equalization payments to the Atlantic provinces. The Budget makes no such provision. It simply reduces the rate of increase in equalization payments to the Atlantic provinces and other provinces. It does not reduce the equalization payments. Indeed, in each fiscal year up to and including 1990 those equalization payments will actually increase rather than be reduced, albeit at a slower rate of increase. Is he aware of the two points to which I made reference?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I thank the Minister for his comments, Mr. Speaker. With regard to his last point I would refer him to Hansard. I thought I was very clear in saying that I understood that there would be no reduction in transfer payments but that there would be an over-all loss from what the transfer payments would have been. The Minister of Finance said very clearly that there would be $2 billion less in transfer payments by 1990. They will go up, but by less than they would have. I thought 1 made it quite clear that I realized they were not going to be decreased.
With regard to liquor, I am pleased that the Minister explained about the cap. I would point out to him that, although the Government raised taxes in Newfoundland, taxes on liquor were put in abeyance for tourists only. If the same measure were taken federally, it would further help the tourism industry. Such a measure has been suggested over the years by groups and associations which are concerned with that particular industry. If he has gone so far as to put a cap on taxes, would he suggest to the Government that it go even further and put taxes for tourists in abeyance in order to bring revenue into the country? I believe, as I think he does, that that is a sunrise industry. There is money to be made in small business through tourism in this country if measures like that are taken.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) raised a number of concerns during his remarks this afternoon. I would like to speak about the other side of the issues that he commented on. He spoke about the fishery in the Atlantic area. I believe he failed to remember some very important things that have happened in recent weeks.
For example, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) recently extended UI benefits to ice-bound fishermen in Newfoundland to ensure that their livelihood would not be lost when they could not get out to the fishing grounds. In the Bill which was recently introduced, the Minister extended the variable entrance requirement for another 19 months. Untill the end of December, 1986 the areas of the
country which are hard-pressed in terms of jobs will be eligible for unemployment insurance with as little as 10 weeks of seasonal employment. The Minister also took steps to freeze premiums for employers during the next period of time so that employers and employees would not be unduly affected. This is particularly important to the fishery.
In looking at the Budget commitments made by the Government to the fishery in Atlantic Canada, I notice that our Government has honoured the commitments of a restructuring agreement for companies like Fisheries Products International and National Sea Products, and in fact something like $138 million is being spent up until March 31, 1985. In looking at what the Government has done for the fishery in Atlantic Canada I need only look at my own Province of Prince Edward Island. The new Minister has given us the appropriate allocation of things we had asked for for years. For the first time we have been let into the Atlantic snow crab fishery. Prince Edward Island has been asking for a part of that resource for many years but was denied it by the Hon. Member's Government. Our new Minister had the foresight and wisdom to know that this resource should be shared in Atlantic Canada. He has given us an opportunity to harvest that resource.
Only several months before the last election, the former Finance Minister of the Liberal Government went so far as to say that the inshore fishery in Atlantic Canada was obsolete and should perhaps be done away with. It is no wonder that Atlantic fishermen decided it was time to make the Government obsolete and turned to a new Government to tackle the problems. Our Government is doing that with the present Budget and the initiatives it has undertaken in the last few months.
The Hon. Member suggested that we might be losing ferries from our transportation system in Atlantic Canada. Nothing could be further from the truth. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) is currently looking at the possibility of constructing two new vessels to serve the Wood Islands-Pictou run between Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. That would, of course, be a great asset to us. Through the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion the federal Government is also considering the possibility of constructing a causeway from New Brunswick to Prince Edward Island.
The Member mentioned concerns about the oil industry and said that we should be providing incentives. However, he forgot to mention the Atlantic Accord. What greater agreement than the Atlantic Accord has been signed between Atlantic Canada and the federal Government in recent times? We also met with the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council this week and were told that it was pleased with this Budget because Atlantic Canada is made up of small businessmen, farmers, fishermen, tourist operators, loggers, foresters, and so on. Those are the people who are being given the opportunity to unleash resources and create jobs and investment in Atlantic Canada. If the Hon. Member took those things into account, he would have to agree that this Budget will be great for Atlantic Canada.
May 30, 1985

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, nothing could be further from the truth. This Budget will have the most serious adverse effect of any economic measure in recent times. It will set the Atlantic Provinces back 20 years. The Government does not have any regional development policy such as has been put in place over the last 20 years in this country. That bias does not exist in this Budget.
I will deal with the specific points starting with the increase in unemployment insurance benefits for fishermen who were trapped by ice. I raised that issue at least twice on the floor of the House of Commons before the Minister eventually announced what I think was too little too late. I was pleased that she extended the variable entrance requirement. She should have made it permanent. The Minister knows that there is no way you can stipulate more than ten weeks in certain parts of the country to make fishermen qualify for unemployment insurance. It was a good idea to extend it for 19 months, but I would like to have seen it extended for 19 years.
With regard to the Government's commitments to the fishery, it is on the record, and the Hon. Member must know it, that $40 million was cut from the fisheries budget in the fall and then a further $25 was cut from the fisheries budget. That will have a negative impact on the Atlantic area.
The Hon. Member talks about the inshore fishery and how the people of Atlantic Canada dealt with this Party as a result of our treatment of the inshore fishery. In Newfoundland, we won 42 per cent of the popular vote and returned three Liberal Members to the House of Commons. That is not a bad record anywhere in the country. That is what the inshore fishermen think of our policy. Indeed, a very strong constituency of ours is among the inshore fishermen.
With regard to APEC, it is on the record and has issued press releases. What the council is saying is a matter of public record. I do not find any group in Atlantic Canada that will disagree that this Budget will have a serious impact on our economy over the next little while.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to join in this debate today, especially when our Government's first Budget is emphasizing our fundamental belief that a strong, healthy and unfettered private sector will bring about economic renewal.
From coast to coast, Canadians have told us that they agree with our initiative. They are willing and able to generate new investment, new business activity and new employment. However, they also told us that they need an environment free of unnecessary government intervention; they need greater access to financial resources for expansion and they need confidence that their hard work will lead to a better life today, tomorrow and every day after.
Moreover, they must believe that their successes will be adequately rewarded. That is why our budget proposals
The Budget-Mr. Warner
emphasize the need for individual initiative and private sector innovation. They must be supported by responsible financial and economic policies that will provide a durable framework for growth.
We have issued a challenge to the thinkers, doers and innovators in the private sector to help us create the jobs that Canadians so badly need. In order to respond to this challenge effectively, an atmosphere of opportunity and stability must exist. Since September 4, the Government has been assisting in creating this environment.
There has always been a shortage of start-up capital to help entrepreneurs with their ideas and putting their ideas into real businesses. Our work with Bill C-23, an Act to amend the Small Businesses Loans Act, guaranteed the continuation of an important source of small business financing.
The life of the Act was extended to March 31, 1990. This longer term established a stable framework for the lenders and the borrowers who use this popular program. This initiative did not increase the size, the role or the power of the Government. Furthermore, our amendment to the Small Businesses Loans Act enhanced both opportunity and stability within the private sector. This is totally consistent with the theme set out in the new Budget.
A further initiative is our work to replace the Foreign Investment Review Agency by Investment Canada. Our message is clear: Canada is open for business again. The Government of Canada is there to assist, not harass, the private sector in creating the new wealth and new jobs that Canada needs.
Historically, the Canadian financial markets have been equity poor. Investment Canada is designed to improve the investment climate and to increase foreign direct investment. We are attempting to create an environment of stability and opportunity, and the injection of new foreign capital will result in new jobs.
Today's reality is that government in Canada has become much too big. It intrudes in the market-place. It inhibits and distorts entrepreneurial activity by sending out false signals to investors. Bill C-15 will reduce government intervention in the economy, an action which is consistent with one of the main objectives set out in the new Budget.
The first Budget of the new Progressive Conservative Government faces head-on the two great problems facing our country-the vicious circle of high unemployment and our spiralling national debt. High deficits constrain our ability to create jobs. High unemployment, in turn, causes even higher deficits. The Budget proposes realistic, fair and effective action to break this vicious circle.
It is centred around three fundamental ideas. First, the Government has become too big. It has become part of the problem instead of being part of the solution. That is why we have been combing Government for waste and inefficiency since September and our efforts are starting to pay off.
We will be lowering government overhead, rationalizing and
improving government programs and selling off Crown corporations which do not serve an essential public policy purpose.

May 30, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Warner
The civil service will be reduced and public sector pensions put on a sounder footing. The search is still on to ensure that we provide maximum value for tax dollars.
Second, future Governments will not be able to support growth and jobs and provide all the services we want if we do not get control of our financial affairs. It is important that Canadians understand the magnitude of our deficit and debt problem and why it poses serious risks to our ability to achieve sustained economic growth.
The public debt is simply the sum of all the past deficits. It took 100 years to accumulate a debt of $18 billion. Now, less than two decades later, the debt is approaching $200 billion and doubling every five years.
Like any borrower, the Canadian Government pays interest on this debt. Like any borrower, the Government has been affected by interest rates. Interest charges have risen from approximately $8 billion per year in the late 1970s to $22 billion last year. When compared to a business situation, it is quite obvious that a borrower such as the Government of Canada, with assets of only approximately $40 billion, is in a situation in which most businesses would be refused loans by lenders. The Government will soon be facing that situation as well if we do not take proper steps to alleviate the problem and eventually solve it. These interest charges have become the fastest growing component of our government expenditures.
Unlike most people, the Government has been borrowing additional funds to pay the interest on past debt. That is why our debt is spiralling out of sight. If we do not show the resolve to deal with this problem, the inevitable result will be paralysis of the Government of Canada.
Third, this Government wants to encourage private initiative. The new capital gains tax exemption challenges Canadians by rewarding success and not subsidizing effort. It will encourage Canadians to invest a part of their savings in new ventures. It will allow the rewards to be enjoyed by the risk takers. We are not asking that every Canadian drain his or her savings account to purchase speculative stocks. Each investor has a different perception of risk and what his or her objectives and goals are for investment. However, the prospect of greater after-tax returns will inevitably shift savings to job creating investments.
The new proposals grant individual Canadians a lifetime capital gains exemption of a half million dollars. The lifetime exemption limit will be phased in over six years beginning with a $20,000 exemption for total capital gains this year, rising to $50,000 next year. It will go up until it reaches an exemption of $500,000. All capital property will qualify for the exemption.
Some earlier speakers have suggested that only 4 per cent of Canadians stand to have capital gains. I believe this is perhaps part of a misconception that some people may have. Many low income earners have capital assets. Many could consider the purchase of capital assets, whether through an investment vehicle such as a mutual fund, through a stock broker purchasing stocks listed on a stock exchange, or perhaps in the form of a cottage or a boat. These are assets which in some cases, over a long period of time, will appreciate and result in capital gains. Whether it is $5,000, $10,000 or $20,000, these are assets already unduly taxed. This tax is a fair tax which will encourage people to invest in situations not only where the risk is relatively low, but perhaps where risk is relatively high, and we have had trouble attracting equity capital in the past.
In the United States, because of favourable capital gains tax, many blue collar workers have seen fit to increase investment in shares of companies they work for and in other shares. The same initiative, I am sure, will be taken by many of our blue collar workers. They will realize that we need more equity capital if we are going to help create those jobs which we so badly need.
The capital gains tax, allowing immediately $500,000 in exemptions for the farm community, recognizes that farmers have traditionally invested a high proportion of their income back into their farms to build up assets which, hopefully, some day they will be able to sell. This sale will provide the funds required for their pension and adequate retirement. It was not too long ago I was speaking with a farmer in my community who had to sell his farm because of health reasons. He made the best deal he possibly could. He took a down-payment and paid off some of the debts he had, but he still had some debts left. After all the paper work had been pretty well done, the tax department came along and levied a capital gains tax on him. This is a capital gains tax which he cannot finance at a bank, a capital gains tax which is jeopardizing what could be a reasonable retirement income from a mortgage that he has. This very unfair tax in a situation like this and many other situations will be terminated and replaced by an incentive which is not only fairer-
I see, Mr. Speaker, that my time has come to an end. I assume I will have a few minutes tomorrow.
